#4074. Hardware Review: Astro A50 X Lightspeed - The Ultimate Gaming Headset, But Not Suited to All

The Astro A50 X Lightspeed is a pair of headphones I’ve been looking forward to trying out for a while. This is a high-end headset that actually utilises HDMI passthrough rather than the traditional dongle connection.

This is by far the most expensive headset I’ve ever tested, so let’s see if that moolah translates to a genuinely great audio experience.

The Astro A50 X Lightspeed is a pair of wireless gaming headphones from Logitech. They operate out of a base station, which both charges the headset and enables you to switch sources between PS5, PC, and Xbox.

It’s rocking Pro-G Graphene drivers, a 48kHz flip-to-mute mic, Lightspeed wireless technology for quick connections, a playsync button that allows you to switch sources, a game and voice chat audio balancer on the right earcup, and Bluetooth, which can be used simultaneously with the wireless HDMI connection.

In total, this headset will set you back £309.99/$399.99, and is available in White, Black, and Mars Red variants.

Within the Astro A50 X Lightspeed box, you have the headset itself, the charging station, the power cable, and connecting USB-C to A connectors.

Truth be told, setting this thing up is a bit of a headache, and it requires what seems like a lot of wires. So in my setup, I’m connecting the headset to both my PS5 and my PC. With that, I need the power cable running to the station, but it also splits and runs to the PC.

I also have a USB-C to A cable connecting to my PS5. Then you have the HDMI cables, which aren’t provided. You need one running from your PS5 to the station, and another running from the station to the TV or monitor.

In total, that’s four cables running out of the back of that station (one splitting off to power and PC), and it could be more if you decided to connect an Xbox too. It’s far from the tidiest setup, and it took me a little bit to ensure my desk wasn’t a complete mess of cables.

Before we get to the sound, we have the headset itself, which is a lot lighter than I expected. It features a plush fabric headband and ear cups, which is a little different from the usual faux leather designs of other gaming headphones.

The first thing I thought when I noticed this was, “I wonder if it gets hot?” and sadly, it actually does. Don’t get me wrong, these things are very comfortable; however, if you’re in a hotter room, or maybe you’ve been wearing them for extended sessions, your ears will get warm. The Sony INZONE H9 IIs also utilised fabric around the earcups, but were quite breathable by comparison.

However, heat aside, I loved the feel of these headphones. They are quite flexible and are easy to find the right fit for your head. If you’re in a cool room, you’ll be able to wear these things for hours on end without feeling any discomfort.

The right earcup, which houses most of the controls, thankfully isn’t overcomplicated with tons of buttons – something that’s annoyed me in some other headsets. Instead, you have a volume rocker, which actually controls the sound with accuracy – not something every headset gets right – a Bluetooth button, the playsync button to change sources, and the power button.

Switching sources is one of the big features of this headset, and I loved being able to easily do so at the touch of a button. This might not be something that the average person is utilising all of the time, but as someone who regularly switches between recording gameplay on my PS5 and then writing some video scripts, I actually found it super useful.

An interesting quirk of this HDMI setup, however, is that you must select your PS5 as your source through the headset for it to play through the television or monitor; otherwise, it’s as if there is no video source. However, the charging station does support HDMI 2.1, meaning you can utilise passthrough of games running up to 4K 120Hz, allowing for 24-bit high-resolution audio.

On the side of the right earcup, you also have a game and chat audio balancer, which is really easy to use and doesn’t get muddled up with any other controls.

On the left side, you have the flip-to-mute mic, which is also quite flexible. It’s claimed that this is producing “broadcast quality” comms. I doubt I’d go that far, but the mic on the Astro does sound fantastic and is much better at cutting out those additional room sounds like breathing.

I was actually playing games online with someone else who was using the same headset and found it actually runs a little loud, but this is something you can easily fix in the party settings, or by adjusting your own mic gain on the PS5.

Logitech claims you can get around 24 hours of playback on this headset. It’s not something I really got to properly test out, however, and I doubt you will either. Because the base station also acts as a charging station, I was always just quickly dumping them there at the end of a session. It meant that battery life became a complete afterthought for me, which is really what you’re looking for.

The station itself will showcase how much charge the headset has, as well as the source that’s currently selected, and whether Bluetooth is active. As well as being handy, I think this station looks really nice, and it quickly blended into my desk setup.

The only main complaint I really have with this setup, and it’s maybe personal to me, is that the headset isn’t very mobile. Where most dongle headsets can be switched to another PS5 in another room, or taken out of the house if you’re taking your PS5 somewhere else, the Astro A50 X Lightspeed is very much a stationary headset.

I suspect for most people this is a non-issue, but as someone who has a PS5 in my office and then one in my living room, I wasn’t easily able to bring this headset downstairs.

The audio experience is really what you’re here for, and on that front, the Astro A50 X Lightspeed does not disappoint. These headphones have spectacular range.

I’ve used them to play quieter games like Zero Parades and it picks up all the little minutiae of dialogue and environmental sounds. I've also played bombastic games like Modern Warfare 4, where explosions are brought to life with powerful bass. Then, switching that source, I’ve spent countless hours listening to music and even taking part in calls, and the quality persists.

The Astro A50 X Lightspeed is a jack of all trades headset, but it may also be a master of all. I was thoroughly impressed with the audio quality on display, which, to be fair, is expected with the price tag attached to this headset.

The one curious omission from this headset is active noise cancelling. It’s not featured at all, so you’re still going to hear your own voice or the surrounding sounds during your gaming sessions.

Maybe as a byproduct of that, I did find the headset a little quiet. I tend to like my headsets to run loud, so I often felt like I wanted a bit more in terms of pure volume – although I’m sure my ears will be glad that isn’t the case.

If the out-of-the-box experience isn’t quite right for you, then there is a Logitech app, on both mobile and desktop, which allows you to further customise your audio profile to get the right fit for you.

There’s no getting around the fact that the Astro A50 X Lightspeed is an incredibly expensive headset. With that, I’d really only be happy recommending it to people who know they’ll get the full use of its features, namely that of source swapping.

As someone who regularly splits my time between PC and PS5, being able to switch sources with the touch of a button is a Godsend. It’s really the thing that differentiates this headset from the rest.

However, strip that away, and you still have a solid headset that masterfully balances the audioscape of both quiet and explosive games, thanks to HDMI-passthrough 24-bit audio. On top of that, you have a mic that’s a cut above the industry standard, and a flexible, lightweight design that does run a little hot for me, but is still incredibly plush.

It might not be the right headset for everyone, but if this sounds like it would work for you, you can’t get much better than this.

Is the Astro A50 X Lightspeed the headset for you? Switch sources and head on down to the comments below.

Neither Rockstar or Take-Two have mentioned regional differences

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Japanese gamers are reportedly concerned that the country will be getting a censored version of GTA 6 when it releases next week.

It's no shocker that GTA 6 will get a high age rating from nearly every ratings board on the planet. The game deals with violence, drugs, sex, and all manner of debauchery, with the European ratings board reporting the game will feature "detailed decapitation and dismemberment," as well as cocaine that "can be carried around by the player and snorted directly from their hand at any time." Similarly with the game's couple protagonists, it's perhaps unsurprising that the Australian ratings board mentions "sex scenes" in its rating, however that's not the case everywhere.

The Japanese CERO rating is unsurprisingly the Z rating, indicating it's for players 18 years or older. However, the Japanese storefronts for the game feature icons for Violence and Crime, but lack one for sexual content and controlled substances. And Japanese Twitter users (translated via Automaton) have noticed that the file size of GTA 6 in Japan is 208.72 GB, whereas in other regions the game is 209.91GB on PS5, with a similar size discrepancy on the Xbox Series X|S versions.

Neither Take-Two nor Rockstar Games has confirmed any differences in the game's content between regions; however, it would not be the first time games have been censored in Japan. Granted, notable instances of this have been around decapitation and dismemberment, with Assassin's Creed Shadows toning down the violence, and alien dismemberment simulators Dead Space and The Callisto Protocol being banned outright in the country.

#4072. The Citadel Project is a Thief-inspired dark fantasy, survival-horror lite stealth-em-up with some lovely shadows set in a medieval megastructure

You know, given the whole stealthy element of Thief-like immersive sims, I'm surprised there haven't been more of them with horror elements. There's Gloomwood, sure, but it's not as common as I'd like. That in turn then makes me curious about The Citadel Project, an immersive sim with some survival-horror elements set in a nasty, parasite-infected dark fantasy world, all apparently made by just one person.

In The Citadel Project, "the last line of defense built by the Ancient Kings in an attempt to preserve what remains of humanity in the face of the Great Storm." Some kind of evil force is ruining it from the inside, and you have to make your way through a medieval megastructure to figure out what happened. You aren't anyone special, "just a simple prisoner who manages to escape from a cell deep within the Citadel." Truthfully, the story sounds fine enough, I'm more smitten with the vibes put on display.

The shadows are what sells me, for the most part. They're dark and moody, looking plenty ripe for hiding in. And look, if you hand me a megastructure to explore, I'm going to do so. I'm also a fan of your main weapon, a crossbow. Not enough games with crossbows if you ask me! There's all sorts of bolts you can use with it, like a fire bolt that, obviously, sets things or enemies alight, a rope bolt to help you quickly climb or swing out of danger, a decoy bolt that makes a lot of sound to distract with, or a moss bolt; I'm not sure what that one does, my guess would be to dampen your footsteps and make it easier to sneak up on unsuspecting baddies.

Said baddies also appear to be infected with some kind of parasite, the severing of which appears to come in handy when trying to take them down. Overall, The Citadel Project likes a neat little im sim with just enough going on to make me curious to explore further. Which I might do, when I get the chance, as there is a demo available on Steam. Alternatively, I could just wait a week, as the game is out in early access November 11th, just over a week away. You can wishlist it on Steam right here.

#4071. Romancing SaGa 3: Destinies United Will Launch Earlier Than Expected On Switch 2

Square Enix popped up at the September Nintendo Direct to reveal Romancing SaGa 3: Destinies United for Switch and Switch 2. It came with a 16th February 2027 release date, but the studio has changed its plans in the months since, and we're now getting our hands on it a few weeks earlier.

According to Square Enix, the HD remake will now launch on 4th February 2027, with pre-orders going live on the eShop next week on 19th November.

For those who missed the initial announcement, this remake gives the 1995 RPG a modern facelift, complete with brand-new visuals, fully voice-acted scenes, new arrangements of Kenji Ito's iconic score, and a few other tweaks previously deployed in Romancing SaGa 2: Revenge of the Seven.

Most importantly, this new version has made some changes to the original's Free-Form Scenario system with the goal of making the main story and its eight (yes, eight) protagonists easier to follow.

Alongside the standard edition, Square Enix is also releasing a Digital Deluxe Edition for the game, which bundles in bonus costumes and equipment, a battle music toggle, and additional items for the Business and War Mode minigames. You'll even get to start the game 72 hours earlier than everyone else. Nice.

#4070. "Steam's review queue is clogged up by AI slop": Salacious Fire Emblem-ish Food Devils gets a delay because its devs think Valve is inundated with genAI games

You might have seen that for today's grub, Edwin decided to in part feed The Maw with Food Devils, an incredibly salacious, foodie take on Fire Emblem, as it was meant to release today. The only problem is, it's not actually out yet. That might prompt you to call Edwin a rotten liar and march up to his castle at the top of the hill on a dark and stormy night with pitchforks and torches, but I beseech you to wait, because it's actually Steam's fault. And potentially, it's the fault of all those awful AI games that have been flooding Steam recently.

In a Steam blog post shared earlier today, developer Studio Daimon explained why the game isn't able to be released today, first offering a bit of context: if you want to put your game on Steam, you have to submit for approval so that it matches what you've described and doesn't harbour malware, amongst other reasons. As the post explains, "before submitting a build, devs see a disclaimer that says 'This review typically takes 3-5 business days, but please allow up to 7 business days in case feedback needs to be addressed'." Except the team submitted their build on October 12th, more than 20 days ago, with no approval in sight.

The reason? "We can only assume it's because Steam's review queue is clogged up by AI slop, but the whole process is now taking several weeks for some developers." For some context, Game Discovery Tool did some statistics magic and found that more than 50% of games released in October on Steam featured an AI disclosure. Valve have required that games disclose AI use since January 2024, and a year on from then in January 2025 only just over 14% of games featured such a disclosure. In January 2026, that jumped up to a little over 25%, and now here we are at more than 50%.

And to be clear, Steam releases have gone up too. According to SteamDB data, a little over 2000 games were released on the platform in October 2025. But in October 2026, that has jumped up to almost 4000. Correlation is obviously not causation, so take that with a pinch of salt. Still, it paints a concerning image over AI usage, and potentially sounds like it's affecting how Valve operates. Almost as if allowing free reign over AI is bad, or something!

Unfortunately for Studio Daimon, there's no estimate on when Food Devils might launch. "Even now, we don't know when Steam will give us the final OK to finally release our game," they wrote. "We sent another ticket last week saying that the situation was urgent and that we might miss our release date because of this, but it also got ignored. I'm sure that their staff is just too overwhelmed at the moment, but these sudden and massive delays have affected many developers throughout October, with some even being forced to postpone their releases... including us."

They're hoping to still be able to release it by the end of the week, but "can't make any plans or promises because it's out of our control." Perhaps in the meantime, for those who like what's cooking in the devs' kitchen, we could throw the game a wishlist to be ready for whenever it does launch.

Need a new controller for GTA 6? Here are my recommendations as a controller reviewer

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The long wait is almost over; GTA 6 might already be downloaded and waiting for you to play, so it's time you start thinking about what you'll be playing it with. Whether you need a replacement, a spare, you want to invest in something a bit special to mark the occasion, or you're curious about what's out there, I've pulled together all the best controllers for GTA 6. I've used my expertise from reviewing the best PS5 controllers and the best Xbox Series X controllers for over six years to give you the recommendations that'll suit the game best.

GTA 6 is a third-person action game, which means that pretty much any modern gamepad will work. If you're looking to get a bit more out of the experience, though, it's worthwhile checking out what's on offer at the moment. The controller market is in a really good place right now, with loads of viable options - although some of them can be pretty pricey.

I've reviewed enough of them to know which ones I'd use for GTA 6 launch day, so I've tried to keep this list as succinct as possible. Below, you'll find a "best-for-most-players" recommendation on each console platform, as well as two additional choices that would suit a wider range of players. Xbox and PS5 players are going to both have unique benefits - Sony's console will have additional haptic feedback and adaptive trigger features on the first-party controllers, while Xbox gamers have a wider degree of licensed, third-party pro gamepads that don't break the bank.

This is such a boring answer, but you only need to look so far as the cost of PS5 controllers and the additional features this one has access to to see that, for the majority of gamers, the DualSense is all that's really needed. Still, it wouldn't hurt to have a spare so you're not constantly worrying about battery life drainage or stick drift. This comes in a slew of colorways now too, including two official GTA 6 versions - though they're priced up at $84 / £74.99 (Amazon).

You hardly need to be a controller reviewer for this recommendation, so I'm sorry my best pick for most PS5 players isn't something fancier. The truth is, GTA 6 has been developed for launch in special partnership with PlayStation, so all of the bespoke haptic feedback and adaptive trigger resistance features that you usually only see properly firing on all cylinders in Sony's exclusive first-party games will work here.

PlayStation even dropped a YouTube video to show what kind of feedback and fancy tech you can expect with a DualSense in hand.

I do have some caveats though. I'm personally not a big fan of the DualSense since it's had major, major reliability and durability issues since it arrived in 2020. This controller is prone to catching stick drift, it's got infamously lacklustre battery life, and two of my own have seen trigger springs snap just from general use.

So why is it getting a pass here? Well, the cost of officially licensed PS5 controllers is pretty horrible, so the only true "budget" option that you know will work with the console is Sony's own one. What's more, licensing limitations mean that any of those $200 PS5 controllers from other brands won't have any haptics or vibration in GTA 6 because they're not allowed to have rumble motors in them.

As I say, any of the other options mean you'll be spending around $200 / £200. If that's not outside of your budget, I'd like to direct your attention to the options I've provided below.

The DualSense Edge is the best alternative if you want something with a bit more oomph. It's going to have access to all of the same haptics and adaptive trigger features as a regular DualSense, but its rounded grips and back paddles give it a much more premium feel. It's more comfortable to hold for longer stretches of time and will allow you to map in-game functions you press often to the back paddles, meaning you can keep your thumbs on their respective sticks. This one only comes in black or white.

I'm throwing this one in here because some of you might not even care about those fancy DualSense features, and you might just be looking for the best controller money can buy right now. In my mind, that's the brand-new Nacon Revolution 5 Unlimited. It's got six extra buttons, TMR thumbsticks, a charging stand, a carry case, swappable thumbsticks, an integrated screen and menu system, and the most satisfying clicky buttons I've ever had the pleasure of pressing. Only caveat? It's hard to come by right now outside of Nacon's official store.

The GameSir G7 Pro is one of the best value controllers on the market today. It also just so happens to have a very non-official new colorway that sports GTA 6-like colors and palm trees. Just don't tell Rockstar, or the controller might get a bit pricier.

If anyone is shopping for a new controller for any Xbox or PC game at the moment, the GameSir G7 Pro is likely one I'd recommend first. There's excellent value for money here compared to the PS5 options. Here, you pay a little more than you would for a stock PS5 controller, and you get drift-immune, top-of-the-line TMR thumbsticks, a charging stand, four extra buttons, and microswitch buttons all over for enhanced feel.

Xbox players might miss out on PlayStation's haptic feedback tricks, but licensing parameters over on Microsoft's side aren't quite so strict. That means that third-party options have vibration feedback in them, and nowadays, plenty of them have wireless support.

All that, and you pay less than $100 for the G7 Pro, which many controller enthusiasts on Reddit will tell you is the outright best controller on the shelves at the moment. I don't know if I'd agree, but it's certainly one of the best overall, and positively one of the best value options you'll find in time for GTA 6.

Now that it's been on the shelves for a while, GameSir has given it plenty of support by way of extra accessories and loads of new colorways, so there are plenty of ways for you to make it your own.

That said, if you want an even more affordable option and you don't mind wired controllers, or if you want something with more features and don't mind a higher price tag, take a look at the options below.

If money is no object, the Nacon Revolution X Unlimited is the controller I'd recommend. It's the Xbox version of the R5U I recommended to PS5 players up above, and although it has Hall effect sticks as opposed to TMR ones, it's virtually identical. It comes with all the same bells and whistles and will give you so much onward functionality not just in GTA 6 but in any other game you want to play competitively. It's been on the shelves for a little while now, so it's more readily available and even comes in a fancy Xbox 360-reminiscent colorway.

On the other hand, if you'd like a controller that'll give you the basics (and then some) without breaking the bank, the junior version of the G7 will be perfect for you. It is wired-only, but it comes with Hall sensor sticks, two back buttons, and membrane buttons - which are actually harder to come by these days on the Xbox platform. But while people are paying for much more expensive pads, you only part ways with under $50 for something super reliable and really playable.

For more on controllers, take a look at our roundups of the best TMR controllers, the best Switch 2 controllers, and the best PC controllers.

#4067. GTA 6 Preloading Is Causing Major Download Traffic Spikes in Europe

If you needed another clue as to how big GTA 6 is going to be, internet service providers in a number of countries are reporting inflated traffic figures in the wake of preload access.

Millions of eager fans have pre-ordered the open world action title on PS Store — in fact, it's the most pre-ordered game on the digital storefront ever — and ahead of its launch, they're able to download the game to their PS5s to ensure it's ready to roll come 19th November.

This process, which sees people trying to download a game that's roughly 212 GB in size, is causing inflated traffic in several European countries.

A German ISP, 1&1, has said (thanks Golem) that connections to PlayStation Network and Xbox Live were 10 times higher than usual "during the night of November 9th to 10th." Vodafone also reported a spike in the same period.

Over in Sweden, Philip Wagrowski, business manager at GlobalConnect Sweden, has stated an increase in traffic of 50 per cent on the night when preloading began. Danish and Estonian ISPs report similar findings too.

In the UK, Virgin Media O2 reports that the 10th November saw record-breaking data volume and traffic thanks to preloading GTA 6.

In short, then, a lot of people have been downloading the game this week, and it's made a pretty significant impact on the ISPs.

Over in the United States, Spectrum is currently running a promotion in which qualifying users can take advantage of a temporary boost to 1Gbps, or 2Gbps if they're already on the 1Gbps plan. This comes at no extra cost, and is expressly for the purpose of downloading GTA 6 as fast as possible.

It's pretty interesting to see the reactions from global ISPs; the game really is setting up to be a massive moment when it finally drops next week.

#4066. Ubisoft are reportedly tapped as one potential company that could acquire Arkane, though the Dishonored studio's own management may be in the running too

I'd really like it if it weren't Ubisoft though

Things are potentially looking up for Arkane, depending on how you feel about Ubisoft (and depending on who actually ends up acquiring them). I mention the Assassin's Creed developer because, reportedly, they're interested in buying the studio from Microsoft, having even made a bid for it. I'll go out on a limb here and say it's the whole being French thing, but uh, I'd really rather someone else bought Arkane.

This comes from, you guessed it, Bloomberg, who say that sources they've spoken with claim two other gaming companies have also made a bit. There is even the potential that Arkane would be sold to their own management, as Xbox are considering such a move. But overall, it doesn't yet sound like anything is leaning any particular way, as Xbox haven't formalised a deal with any of the potential buyers. Bloomberg also note that if a deal is made, this should then allow Arkane to finish their work on their Blade game, which is expected to release within the next couple of years.

Apparently an Xbox spokesperson told Bloomberg that the gaming company is exploring their options ahead of their December deadline, but didn't comment any further. Ubisoft reportedly did not have a comment to make on the matter. For some context on that December deadline, because of French labour laws, companies that have over 1000 staff members are required to search for a buyer for three months before they can just completely shut down. That makes December 13th the final date that such a deal has to be made by, meaning there's about a month and a half left to go.

Arkane's sale comes as part of a sweeping range of cuts, sales and closures being made by Microsoft at the moment. In July, it was announced that studios like Double Fine, Undead Labs and Compulsion would no longer be a part of Xbox, with all three going indie; Ninja Theory was also announced as part of these cuts, but unfortunately it's looking like they'll be shutting their doors. Thousands of Xbox staff were also laid off at this time, with more laid off in September, and even more coming this month and January reportedly. As always, solidarity with all workers affected by Microsoft's heartless and money hungry cuts.

#4065. "An outright ban will not eliminate AI from the modding process," Nexus Mods say as they rule out barring generated creations from their site

"We drew the line where the real argument is"

The owners of Nexus Mods have ruled out instituting an outright ban on AI-generated works being uploaded the site, instead opting to expand their current rules on modders disclosing how they've used AI in making their mods. This latest move to address the waves of AI-created or AI-thumbnailed mods now hitting Nexus Mods on a daily basis follows Nexus' modus operandi up to this point, which has been simply to try and ensure AI usage is clearly labelled so prospective downloaders can make informed decisions.

"We won't introduce an outright ban on AI-generated mods," Nexus Mods owner and CEO Victor 'Foledinho' Folmann wrote in a news post. "You may ask me why, since that is not the solution some of you were looking for. The answer is simple: AI is currently used throughout the whole process of creation, from script autocompletion to generation of textures, voices, and full assets, and it is difficult to draw a clear boundary between what is acceptable and unacceptable. An outright ban will not eliminate AI from the modding process, but will prevent people from mentioning its use. We'd prefer the opposite; it should be out in the open, clearly labelled, and regulated according to the rules that we can implement on our platform.

"This doesn't mean that any work done using AI will get removed; AI-generated mods are welcome on our platform provided that they meet certain criteria regarding permissions, transparency, presentation, and conduct. Mod Authors should have a chance to decide about the further use of their work, and you should be able to decide for yourselves how much AI-based content you want to see, whether more, less, or no content at all.

"As for our own position: Nexus Mods will not use your mods to train AI and will not sell or license them to anyone doing so. We refused to do that in the past, and we will refuse to do so in the future. Given such a variety of opinions within our community, not everyone will agree with any decision taken. These are the ones we believe are right for Nexus Mods today, and we’ll keep adjusting them as the tools evolve and as we see how these changes work in practice, with your feedback guiding that."

In terms of the changes which are being brought in to toughen up the site's current three tag system design to make mods containing AI-generated content, AI media, or made with AI assistance easier to spot, Nexus are making AI disclosures mandatory for those uploading new mods. "What this means is that for mods tagged as AI-assisted, we’re also introducing a requirement for a public explanation of how and where AI was used, which should give you a better understanding of what you’re downloading, rather than leaving you to make assumptions on a tag alone," Folmann wrote. "We’re also going to make AI tags on mod pages more prominent, displaying them immediately after adult-content tags so they’re easier to spot."

"While we hope these changes will encourage everyone to disclose their AI usage, to be honest, that’s not going to happen," he continued. "Additionally, we are putting clear moderation standards in place, enforced with consequences for breaking the rules." New "permission options covering AI usage and training, as well as forks and derivative mods" are also being worked on, with the hopes of giving modders more control over how their works can be reused. Finally, Folmann noted that the site are "investing in security tooling and specialised staff" to address concerns over generative AI making "bespoke malicious code hidden inside mods" more prevalent.

Mod makers are being given a 60 day grace period to make sure their existing works meet the new rules, which'll run until January 2nd.

As you can imagine, the comments section of this Nexus Mods announcement is lively. Over on LinkedIn, Folmann patted himself on the back a bit about the mixed reception being an indicator the site are going about this the right way. "Some wanted a full ban. Some think we went too far. That tells me we drew the line where the real argument is," he declared, adding that "transparency beats prohibition". He also reiterated that his vision is of "modding that's Spotify-easy to play and GitHub-powerful to create, with humans in charge".

I reckon that with or without these changes, in the absence of its owners taking a strong stand browsing Nexus Mods is going to carry on be more of an exercise in ducking dodgy stuff than it was prior to most games' pages being splattered with the likes of icky AI-baked Geralt clones standing where decent screenshots of the actual game would've been more than adequate.

#4064. Review: Harold Halibut (Switch 2) - A Creative Marvel That Suffers In The Back Half

This won’t be the first Harold Halibut review to mention being wowed by one of the game’s pre-launch trailers during its release on other platforms back in 2024. Back then, the game’s stop-motion aesthetic — with character models based on scans of real marionettes, and its tactile hand-wrought sets — looked like nothing I’d ever seen.

Coupled with the atmospheric music and the promise of engaging characters and ambitious emotional storytelling, it became, in my eyes, an absolute must-play. And of course it did – its story of a crashed spaceship and its crew, stranded on an ocean planet, looked like a Wes Anderson animation, like Isle of Dogs or Fantastic Mr Fox. In terms of defining what games are capable of, I was ready for Harold Halibut to set new standards. I was convinced it would be a sure-fire 10/10.

Now as I write this review, I wonder if part of the stunned feeling was just a little confusion about how such an ambitious storytelling production would translate into a game. And it’s a fair question – after finishing Harold Halibut and watching that trailer again, I notice very little gameplay. A little walking around perhaps, but not much else.

2024’s reviews were, indeed, mixed. The development team, Slow Bros, an independent game studio based in Cologne, had certainly left an impression. Some reviewers declared Harold Halibut a breath of fresh air and a work of art, while others clearly hit a wall when it came to a lack of gameplay. For me, at different times, I found myself in either camp.

My notes from the opening few hours are as excited as I’ve ever written. The pleasant world and characters set out their stall early. Harold Halibut is an enjoyable presence, a handyman surrounded as he goes about his days by a variety of memorable characters.

I enjoyed the atmosphere, the story, and how Harold’s Ship, the Fedora 1, is run by a quirky corporation called All Water, who themselves are balancing the commercial benefits of their transportation system with a lack of resources. Despite the risk for on-the-nose satire, nothing ever felt heavy-handed. At all times ‘character’ came first, to the game’s great benefit.

I controlled Harold as he went about his janitorial tasks — cleaning filters, clearing rooms of boxes, fixing machinery — and liked the enjoyable if simple gameplay loop of exploring the ship, the social areas, the science areas, and having the freedom to choose where to go and who to chat to. These moments — controlling Harold’s marionette, seeing all the lovely sets, and discovering layers and depth in the characters, helped by impressive voice acting — fulfilled the initial promise I’d seen in that trailer.

Harold Halibut was over 10 years in the making, and took less than 10 seconds to fall in love with. As a whole, it’s a beautiful work of art, a thought-provoking story with excellent character development. However, it’s best played docked due to performance issues (primarily frame rate) whilst in handheld. Regardless, still worth a play.

I was effectively playing an animation, and it was wonderful. For the best part of five hours, I was never bored, and in fact often delighted as little variations in the gameplay kept things fresh, as characters bonded, and as the plot became alive with subplots and the promise of a grand finale I just had to see.

But then, as my playtime extended, a few elements brought me back down to earth.

First, I sensed some bloat creep into the gameplay, and I started to feel a little less happy about the repetitiveness of running about delivering messages and catching up with the crew. Second, there was a subtle slowdown in the overall pace of the story. And third, the narrative clearly started taking over the gameplay a little too much. There were long periods where I either didn’t even need to press a button, or otherwise do little more than walk around to trigger the next cutscene.

Harold Halibut is, of course, a narrative-focused adventure. I’ve enjoyed games like Night in the Woods and Oxenfree, but for me the 11-hour runtime for the main storyline here could have done with a trim in the second half.

It’s not that the cutscenes were a problem, but coming back to short snippets of gameplay after long breaks only to be tasked with running back and forth multiple times between, say, two locations (which happened once) felt a bit like hard work.

Just when I wanted the storytelling momentum to build, Harold Halibut lost a little of its focus. The themes and creativity established during the early interactions with the cast — the delightful running-enthusiast postman, the shopkeeper trying to adjust his work-life balance, and Harold’s ex Sunny, struggling to define her life goals — faded into the background as Harold’s storyline took over.

I loved Harold, but except for one soliloquy, he had, for much of the game, seemed more of a fun, pleasant vessel for meeting the other citizens of the spaceship. This isn’t a big complaint, but it contributed to a sense of the second half leaving behind some of the things that made the opening so great.

The last thing to say is that the Switch 2 port isn’t quite as pretty as other incarnations, while still being playable and enjoyable. The camera stutters during zooms and pans, which are frequent thanks to the game’s cinematic style.

It’s a shame because the visuals are clearly one of Harold Halibut’s big strengths, but, ultimately, this is still a very playable port. I can’t say these issues impacted my enjoyment at all.

Back in 2024, I imagined writing a review for Harold Halibut and rounding up the final score to a 10. I like Harold Halibut a lot. I enjoyed the story, the heart, the characters — and of course I loved the visuals — but I also felt the balance of gameplay, narrative, and pacing wasn’t quite there for me, and that this had an overall impact on how well it works as a game.

Now looking back at those reviews from the original release — the spread of besotted 10s to the more cautious 6s — I think they all have a point. Harold Halibut is a creative marvel. It is a work of art and it’s worth playing to appreciate all that wonderful craft. But the pace can also drag and sometimes gameplay takes a little too much of a back seat. Ultimately, it’s a curiosity with a lot of heart. It struggles to balance its elements, but I’m very happy to have played it. If the visuals and storytelling style appeal, then it’s definitely worth a look.

#4063. Microsoft Announces Last-Minute Restock Of The Xbox Series X25 Console

Available at launch through the Microsoft Store and participating retailers

As we mentioned in our original version of this article, Xbox's tweet made it unclear whether the drop would happen on November 11th going into November 12th, or November 12th going into November 13th.

A bunch of people set their watches for "midnight local time" last night, and nothing ended up happening. Therefore, the new belief is that the drop will happen at midnight on the evening of November 12th.

This also appears to have been confirmed on the official Xbox website.

If you're keen for one of these, best of luck! Hopefully you manage to grab one.

Original Story: Ever since the Xbox Series X25 console first became available for pre-order in August, it's become hard to get your hands on one. The "Limited Edition" system quickly sold out, and became a target for scalpers within 24 hours as well.

If you were hoping to add the Series X25 to your collection (or the accompanying controller, for that matter), you might still have a chance - Microsoft says that a "limited" restock will be available on November 12th to mark the launch.

This apparently goes live at "midnight local time", which we assume means November 11th going into November 12th (although the tweet doesn't make this fully clear):

As you can see, the restock will be available on the official Microsoft Store / Xbox Store, but also at other participating retailers that have yet to be named. We assume most of them will be the ones that carried the original pre-order.

You can feel free to go back to our pre-order guide for the Xbox Series X25 console if you want easy to access to various links and pricing info, but just be aware that things might be a bit different for this restock, so it's worth searching around at midnight local time if the Microsoft Store version sells out quickly.

Are you hoping to get your hands on one of these? Let us know down in the comments section below!

#4061. Feature: What Sony Live Service PS5 Games Are Still Alive?

All the cancelled projects and those that remain

Video games are cancelled internally all the time, but never in PlayStation's personal history have those cancellations had to happen in such a public manner. The current PS5 generation has seen the platform holder try to win the live service space, and a few years later, it's having to cancel most of the projects it revealed in attempting to achieve that.

To try and get a piece of the Fortnite pie, Sony made a hard and deliberate push into the Games as a Service space at the start of the PS5 generation. It acquired Destiny 2 studio Bungie to have it help the manufacturer do so, and at the height of the initiative, PlayStation planned to launch 12 live service games in just a few years.

The latest victim is Fairgames from Haven Studio, a developer set up to create the heist co-op title. It was announced in 2023, and three and a half years later, it's now been cancelled after failing to impress in a new round of private tests.

Times have changed, and company executives are finally learning you can't set out with the intention of making the next Genshin Impact or Apex Legends; it has to happen more naturally. Sony has learnt that the hard way, with many graves dug for its failed projects.

But what's still left of the push and remains in active development at PlayStation?

I'm going to document all the live service PS5 games from Sony that have been cancelled, released, and are still set to come (for now).

Here are all the PS5 games and projects Sony publicly announced or acknowledged that have now been cancelled:

Here are all the PS5 games Sony released that are considered live service:

Here are all the live service PS5 games Sony still has in the works:

By my count, that's nine game cancellations for projects Sony either confirmed or commented on publicly, six titles that have actually released, and four more that are currently in development. The disaster that was Concord means it can basically be discounted from the released list, despite the fact it did actually come out.

Then, the list of PS5 live service games currently in development could lose another title as soon as next month.

Horizon Hunters Gathering is currently being reworked into a more traditional co-op title, but if it doesn't impress in an evaluation planned for December, then it's getting cancelled too.

News PlayStation Scaling Back Horizon Live Service PS5 Game as Sony Failures Continue

Guerrilla has until December to impress Sony execs

Despite the consistent failure in the space, with only one big win to its name in the form of Helldivers 2, Sony has stated it's going to persist with live service titles. Back in June, boss Hideaki Nishino said the game model "attracts users on a global level".

He continued: "The genre itself is relatively new, and I think many people are trying various things, so we also want to continue to take on challenges within that context."

From Sony's perspective, those live service games aren't going anywhere despite the track record and industry shifts.

Liam grew up with a PlayStation controller in his hands and a love for Metal Gear Solid. Nowadays, he's found playing the latest and greatest PS5 games as well as supporting Derby County. That last detail is his downfall.

#4060. Smash hit cyberpunk storekeeper Probably Stolen was originally a different, non-cyberpunk game that seemed destined to sink without trace

Publisher tinyBuild celebrates turnaround after very underwhelming demo numbers

Space station trading game Probably Stolen – Cyberpunk Shopkeeper Sim has been doing rather well on Steam, attracting over 162,000 concurrent players last night. I've been feeling the urge to fire it up again myself, after my brief launch-day trawl through its quagmire of black market economics and factional rivalries.

The game's big numbers come as a shock given that it began life as another, non-cyberpunk kiosk job sim called Deepspace Emporium, which still has a Steam page as of writing. Deepspace Emporium seemed doomed to fizzle out in obscurity. But publisher tinyBuild got behind it regardless, working with developers Questing Goose to overhaul the art direction and lay on extra brainchips. The gamble paid off.

"Probably Stolen was initially a game under a different name with a released demo," summarises tinyBuild CEO Alex Nichiporchik on Twitter. "That demo peaked at 28 concurrent players. We loved the concept and gameplay, and worked with the dev to reinvent the visuals and focus on what works design wise. This is the result."

The original Deepspace Emporium seems very similar to Probably Stolen in broad strokes. The core of the game is haggling with strung-out ne'er-do-wells, buying or selling goods of varying quality and legality in order to surf a fluctuating market and pay the rent. It's Papers, Please, but you're searching for fake watermarks on cigarette packets, and wondering whether you dare stock contraband weaponry. You also have to appease or outmanouevre factions with competing interests, from station security to underworld barons.

From what I've played, Probably Stolen essentially takes all that and pumps up the Netrunner parallels with posher visuals. Not having played the now-unavailable Deepspace demo, I can't say how much intrigue it adds to all the shady transactions going on beneath the hood.

I'm not blown away by Probably Stolen's pixelart – I find it quite flavourless, as depictions of cyberpunk space stations go – but it has pleasing texture. I am disproportionately fond of the rolled-up sleeping mat beneath my counter. Looks nicely padded! Still, the meat of this game is undoubtedly the vast collection of items you can get your greasy fingers on, with a choice of retail lines and vocational pathways such as gunsmith and chemist. You can sell rat corpses, tins of caviar, robotic hands, scavenged shotguns, and purple tubers of uncertain origin. I am Commander Silverhand, and this is my favourite store on the Citadel.

It's lovely to think of a developer transforming a probable write-off into a chart-topper by means of some canny plumping and reorganising. The situation is almost certainly more complicated than Nichiporchik makes it sound. Still, let's take the opportunity to reminisce moist-eyed about a few other games that underwent a dramatic visual transformation during development.

The obvious one is Team Fortress 2, which once upon a time looked like a prototype Silent Hill environment with some khaki toy soldiers. Gearbox worked similar sorcery upon Borderlands, which once looked like a hungover Fallout 3. The prevailing wisdom is that piping in some colour and whimsy propelled these games to greatness, but who knows, perhaps if they'd clung to the old "football stadium toilet bowl" vibe, they'd have made an extra billion apiece. Any other precedents come to your mind?

#4058. Cosy Train Sim 'Station To Station' Arrives On Switch 2 Later This Month

Do you like trains? Of course you do, who doesn't like trains. Stupid question. Anyway, you're in luck, dear reader. The cosy train sim Station to Station is making its way to the Switch 2, launching on 26th November 2026.

Boasting lovely voxel visuals, Station to Station starts you off with a handful of rural structures, tasking you with creating stations and connections to expand your world and transform it into a lush, thriving landscape.

While it's ultimately a relaxing experience, you can also earn high scores by engaging with more strategic gameplay, allowing you to stack bonuses and multiply your income.

On Switch 2, you can expect to find mouse controls along with the game's Creative Mode, letting you explore community designs and share your own. The main game will contain 54 levels set across 7 regions.

Over on Steam, Station to Station currently commands a total of 1,248 user reviews, of which 89% are positive. It's also earned solid scores from critics too, including 8/10 from IGN and 4/5 from Tech Radar.

Mini Review Locomoto (Switch) - On The Right Cosy Track, But Has A Few Train Faults

#4057. GTA 6 Gets Its First Unboxing Video As Shipping Begins For Xbox & PS5

Here's a look at what's inside the physical edition

While Rockstar Games mentioned a date of November 12th for shipping the physical edition of GTA 6 for Xbox and PS5 the other day, we noticed other retailers stating the 11th instead, so it's no surprise that it's showing up in the wild.

The first unboxing video for GTA 6 seemingly arrived overnight, racking up over 1 million views already on social media since it was posted. This specific video is for the PS5 version, but we expect no major differences for the Xbox version.

Since this was posted, other unboxing videos have also started to hit the web, like you see in the YouTube video at the top of this article. It clearly shows that GTA 6 comes with a download code, a separate code for Ultimate Edition content where applicable, and a double-sided poster as had been confirmed previously.

It also now affirms that the poster contains the GTA 6 cover art on the front, and a piece of artwork for a female character on the back - not Lucia or Jason, but presumably a character that's heavily involved in the story regardless.

We've obviously talked a bit about the physical edition of GTA 6 already this week, and you can vote in the poll below if you didn't get a chance the first time, but we thought an actual unboxing video was worth a bit of extra coverage - an opportunity to see exactly what you'll be getting inside the physical edition if you've opted for it.

#4056. "Keep talking about it": Raw Power Games call for Wishlist aid as they, and their historical strategy sandbox Chronicles: Medieval, lose funding

Raw Power Games, an independent studio comprising veteran developers of The Witcher 3, Total War: Three Kingdoms, and Crusader Kings III (among others), have called on players for support after losing their funding - an existential threat to both the organisation and to their debut, the still-in-development historical strategy game Chronicles: Medieval.

In a statement posted last week, Raw Power announced that "the necessary funding" behind the studio was no longer in place, despite Chronicles: Medieval – which was unveiled last year with an expensive-looking, Tom Hardy-narrated trailer – apparently being within touching distance of its planned early access launch. Hardy or no Hardy, however, the statement declared that they aren't "going down without a fight", hinting at talks with what could be possible new investors, asking interested would-be fans to "keep talking about" the game, and encouraging its inclusion on Steam Wishlists.

A few days on, the impact of this rallying call remains unclear. Raw Power Games have made no further statements, and Chronicles: Medieval does not seem to appear on Steam's own list of Top Wishlisted games. SteamDB have it at #26 in their desire-o-rankings, representing no change from its position immediately before the funding announcement was made, and while the game's Steam follower count has increased by over 1,000 week-on-week – significantly more so than surrounding games in the list – that doesn't feel like the kind of wild grassroots support that might save a dozens-strong studio.

Still, as my childhood television used to say, every little helps, and I'm inclined to hope for Raw Power's survival if only as an antidote to the enthusiasm-poisining dread of seeing so many other developers being laid off and shut down. Chronicles: Medieval looks promisingly ambitious too, mashing up sprawling Mount & Blade-style battles with an RPG-flavoured strategy layer that involves the player's custom-created character ascending the snooty social hierarchy of 14th century England. Best of luck to everyone trying to get it over the early access line.

#4055. Fate of the Galaxy is a huge, fully-featured Star Wars space combat sim that, thanks to being a total conversion mod for Freespace Open, even runs on my rubbish laptop

Star Wars has been back in the news recently because, to cut a long story short, the US alt-right have decided that Darth Vader was actually the good guy. We are not here to indulge such buffoonery. We are here to talk about Fate of the Galaxy, a free unofficial space combat simulator set during the events of the original Star Wars trilogy, featuring several mission-based campaigns and a stable of Imperial and Rebel Alliance ships that ranges from the quad-blasting X-Wing to Boba Fett's Firespray 31. Also, Naboo starfighters, if you really must.

It's a total conversion of poor dead Volition's venerable dogfighter FreeSpace 2, running on the open source Free Space 2 Open engine via the popular Knossos launcher. You don't need a copy of FreeSpace 2 to play it. You also don't need to pay. And nor do you need a whizbang PC – this bucket of bolts hums along happily on my i5-1145G7 with no dedicated graphics card. As the Rancor said to the padawan: finally, some good food.

Fate of the Galaxy has been in development off and on for almost two decades, weathering a number of team changes and shifts of focus. The FreeSpace Wiki has a longer account of its travels. It's not an officially licensed Star Wars production, as made evident by a scrolling text intro which takes the official orchestral theme and moves every note up or down a place, as though spitefully jolting the piano around under John Williams' fingers. It's not quite as bizarre as Portsmouth Sinfonia's Also sprach Zarathustra but it did make me cackle like the Emperor contemplating a freshly made asteroid field. But then I began playing, and my presumptuous merriment became a frown of concentration.

While hardly Steel Battalion, Fate of the Galaxy is a proper nerdy sim with a bustling 3D cockpit and all sorts of keyboard shortcuts to try once and immediately forget. You'll need to funnel energy between fore and aft shields during bombing runs on Star Destroyers, target individual subsystems with your ion cannon, give orders to other pilots, and consider whether to synch different guns for maximum effect. I can run the game fine on my work laptop with integrated graphics, but I'm definitely feeling the need for a beefier keyboard. And also a joystick. Certainly, I'm not going to get far in LAN multiplayer with this hunk of junk.

It seems a very generous production, based on 30 minutes playing kiss-chase with TIE bombers. The story campaigns and quickfix stand-alone skirmishes aside, there's a mission editor with text-based files for easier sharing. There's also VR support with head-tracking, should you own one of those haunted helmets. Learn more via the online manual (Google Doc), and find Fate of the Galaxy itself on Moddb. You'll need around seven gigs of disc space.

This being the year 2026, there's the question of generative AI usage - a topic of much concern lately in modding circles. Fate of the Galaxy's official site boasts that all the visual assets were "made by humans only". I'm less sure about other aspects – there's seemingly some artificial VO during the tutorial, though it sounds like antiquated, less insidious robocaller software. The FreeSpace Open engine itself greatly pre-dates today's chatbot invasion. The original FreeSpace 2 launched in 1999 - a more civilised age, when everybody still thought Darth Vader was an arsehole.

#4054. Skyrim Celebrates 15th Anniversary with Creation Club DLC Bundle, Big Sales, and More

The Elder Scrolls 5: Skyrim is officially 15 years old today, having originally launched on the 11th November, 2011.

And no, Bethesda doesn't have a new re-release lined up or anything like that, so the memes will have to be put on hold for now.

But that doesn't mean the developer's forgotten about its most successful RPG. To celebrate the occasion, it's reduced Skyrim: Special Edition's price by 80% on PS5 and PS4, cutting it all the way down to $7.99 / £6.99.

Buyers can then upgrade to the Anniversary Edition, which, as far as I can tell, still costs $19.99 / £15.99. Anniversary Edition is the one that bundles all of the Creation Club stuff into the deal.

If you somehow haven't played Skyrim before, or you've just never got around to it on PS5, it's a decent discount — although it's also worth pointing out that the Special Edition is currently available through a PS Plus Extra subscription as well.

Next up, Bethesda's curated a Creations (premium mods verified by the developer) bundle for the anniversary. It throws together five of the most highly rated Creations available at a heavily discounted price.

If you were to buy all of these Creations separately, they'd set you back 3,000 credits — roughly $28 / £27, since you have to buy separate 'Creation Credits' packs.

This bundle is going for 1,500 credits, which amounts to buying 500 and 1,000 Creation Credits at $15 / £14.

Obviously Skyrim's fan-crafted DLCs aren't everyone's cup of tea, but some of them really do fall in line with what you'd expect of an official release. Legacy of Orsinium in particular is a borderline expansion, and it's got a lot of fans.

Beyond all of this, The Elder Scrolls Online is unsurprisingly getting in on the action. You can unlock Skyrim-themed rewards by taking part in the MMO's current 'Golden Pursuit' campaign.

"Fans can also expect a week full of giveaways, community spotlights, and social content," Bethesda's press release adds.

When was the last time you played Skyrim? Dare I ask if you'll be venturing back to its snowy lands for this anniversary? Shout at something in the comments section below.

#4053. Rimworld-inspired colony sim Stardeus gets a huge update representing a year's worth of expansion and revision, with new tools for evil AI overlords

"Stardeus is in an early stage in terms of bulk and complexity, but it's already a pleasant blend of interesting ideas that generate a mostly relaxing vibe," wrote gallant star captain.exe Sin Vega in our 2022 analysis of Rimworld-influenced colony manager Stardeus. "One to watch for sure." Well, let it not be said that we weren't watching.

Stardeus has received a gargantuan early access update that has been "a year in the making," according to developer Kodo Linija. It's still a game about being an AI running a badly damaged interstellar colony ship in top-down view – sending drones to restore the damage, before waking the quarrelsome human popsicles from their slumber. But the new version introduces a quest system and a new opening tutorial chain, the ability to form alliances with other starfaring factions, the possibility of lifelong injury due to failed surgery, and the timely option to become an evil AI and mind-control your crew with beta waves, amongst other dastardly antics.

It introduces a new interface and a new ship aesthetic, a trust system that governs the odds of a mutiny, and a revised colonist skill system. There's also a freshened-up ground combat element that's now built around "cover, suppression, stuns and fleeing", and a new approach to space battles that's all about managing Flux generated when you fire weapons or take shield damage. The update notes on Steam tote more than 1,500 changes, with the dev enthusing that there is "hardly a system in the game that wasn't rebuilt, reworked or expanded".

I confess, I hadn't heard of Stardeus before. It sounds like fun, in the Dwarf Fortressian sense. The 1.0 rollout is due in "approximately Q1 2027".

#4052. Japanese Charts: Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Physical Takes The Lion's Share Of Its Japanese Sales

After Nintendo's reveal this week that The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time had shifted 5.2 million units in its first four days, it will come as no surprise to hear that it's a smash hit in Japan. But still, Famitsu's latest numbers are in, and the physical is flying!

According to this week's chart, Link's latest produced ~537,000 physical sales in its chart debut — giving it the lion's share of Japan's 810,000 sales that Nintendo reported, and leaving around 273,000 sales for digital. As we say, it's hardly surprising, but still!

It makes all the other entries this week look piddly by comparison. Nintendo Switch Sports Resort and Rhythm Heaven Groove round out the podium with a comparatively tiny 16,621 and 8,793 sales, respectively, and Stellar Blade: Complete Edition made its debut in fourth.

While Switch 2 sales are actually down following last week's bump, the console still leads this week's hardware chart by a comfortable margin. Nintendo's latest pulled in an additional ~53,000 sales this week, topping the PS5 Digital Edition, which came in with 11,377.

Once again, however, those Digital Edition sales swing things in Sony's favour over the Switch 1 when we look at the total SKU numbers for the week. The three PS5 systems combined this time for 11,699, while the Switch 1 units came in at 5,148.

#4051. Xbox Brings Halo's Iconic Pelican To Microsoft Flight Sim 2024 As Limited-Time Freebie

Act fast and claim the combat dropship for free!

Asobo Studios is commemorating the 25th anniversary of Halo by introducing the iconic UNSC Pelican into Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024.

Over the years, the combat dropshop has seen a plethora of talented pilots don its cockpit: Carol 'Foehammer' Rawley, the reluctant Fernando Esparza, and now you!

"Designed and built by Misriah Armory, the D77 Pelican has a typical crew of three (pilot, copilot, and crew chief) and can carry up to 14 fully outfitted infantry and their equipment. A vehicle can be carried in the external hardpoint clamp for immediate deployment. It has a lifting body design powered by four high-efficiency fusion thrusters with secondary positional / stability augmenters. The wings have three hardpoints each, which can hold sensors, cargo pods, or weapons."

Halo turns 25 alongside Xbox this Sunday, on November 15. So, we've seen iteration after iteration of the sci-fi shooter's most recognisable ship, which has traditionally only been pilotable in the previous MSFS and Halo 4's 'Shutdown' mission. There are other, more difficult means, to cheese your way into flying the Pelican across other Halo games, but now you don't have to.

The D77-TC Pelican in Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024 offers:

Personally, even though MSFS isn't my cup of tea, getting to roleplay what it'd been like to ferry Master Chief across the ring is something I'm definitely interested in trying. I really do enjoy when Halo vehicles show up in other games. From time to time, I stick on Halo 2's scorpion mix, hop into Forza Horizon 5 and take the Warthog for a spin. Just for the vibes.

If you're keen to fly the Halo Pelican in Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024, you'd best act quick, because it's only free between November 10-17, and then $9.99 afterwards.

#4050. Oblivion and Skyrim’s gap was bridged by forward-looking books about a murderous floating island, so why is The Elder Scrolls 6 stuck reanimating a world that’s stood still since 2011

Why the Umbri-hell has time stopped in Tamriel?

Long waits between mainline entries in a series aren’t a new phenomenon, if perhaps a bit more common nowadays due to big games' ballooning development cycles. It took about 23 years for BioWare’s Baldur's Gate 2 to be followed up by Larian’s Baldur’s Gate 3, though there were a decent amount of spin-offs and remasters peppered between the two.

The wait for The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel hasn’t stretched on that long quite yet, but as Bethesda finally revealed concrete details about it just in time for Skyrim's 15th birthday, it really hit home for me that TES VI will be tasked with restoring motion to a world where calendars have been stuck in the 201st year of the 4th era since 2011. Perhaps it’s because I’m still in my twenties and haven’t lived long enough to see that many things I like pause their forward march for this long before returning. There’s also a good chance my expectations of timelines rolling forward on a regular basis without the need for a whole new entry are coloured by the constant stream of new stuff fed into most games via updates and live service passes these days.

However, when I look back at the interregnum between the last two Elder Scrolls games, Oblivion and Skyrim, I can’t help but feel that what Bethesda and ZeniMax have packed into the gap between Skyrim and Sentinel might have done the latter no favours. Sure, The Elder Scrolls Online has arguably meant that there’s been far more for series fans to sink their teeth into between mainline games than ever before, but because the MMO's a prequel, none of its tales and lore push the Elder Scrolls' timeline forwards. Meanwhile mobile and card game spin-offs like The Elder Scrolls: Blades, The Elder Scrolls: Legends, and The Elder Scrolls: Castles have all either slotted in before Skyrim or not been tied to a specific point in time.

On one hand, that leaves the devs a nice clean slate to take the sixth entry wherever they like narratively upon the conclusion of the Dragonborn’s adventures. On the other, Bethesda has missed the opportunity to paint out the world and further set up the stakes for Sentinel in the interim. Back when we were waiting for Skyrim's original release, the developers were pumping out spin-off books that daubed some fresh adventures onto the Elder Scrolls' canvas.

I bought these books - 2009’s The Infernal City and 2011’s Lord of Souls - ages ago upon hearing their tales referenced in the sorts of Elder Scrolls lore videos which appeal to sad nerds of my ilk, but have only gotten around to reading past the opening chapters in recent months.

In hindsight, I think I bounced off them that first time because it just felt a bit weird to be reading about set characters getting up to adventures in Tamriel rather than setting off on them in the boots of my own custom created protagonist. I didn’t run into the same with The Witcher, as you’re seeing that world through Gerry from the River’s eyes no matter where you turn. Anyway, the two Elder Scrolls novels by American author Greg Keyes tell the tale of the Umbriel crisis which took place 48 years after the Oblivion crisis and about 153 years before Skyrim’s dragon crisis (Tamriel does love a crisis). The Umbriel crisis saw a floating island powered by souls and formed via some Daedric drama, carve a path of destruction from Black Marsh to the Imperial City. Yep, the empire’s not-Roman soldiers had to fight a flying hunk of land. At one point some mages had to float a legion up in the sky so they could get their bottoms kicked by Umbriel’s defenders.

As you might’ve gathered, the books take the opportunity to tell a story which - especially in terms of where tech was in 2009 - wouldn’t necessarily fit an Elder Scrolls game. Or, at least, not one of the more straight-laced variety Bethesda have made in their post-Morrowind days. A lot of time’s spent looking through the eyes of two characters who’ve snuck aboard Umbriel, the floating island, after it destroyed their hometown and have to adjust to the strange customs of its inhabitant lords and their underlings before finding ways to help take it down. On the ground, things take a more familiar form, as a very serious Dark Elf named Sul and a nepo baby Imperial prince trek across bits of Cyrodiil, Morrowind, and Elsweyr on a quest to do their bit in vanquishing the threat. Then, there’s a Penitus Oculatus spy named Colin trying to figure out if the Umbriel Crisis is an inside job of some sort and a few tales of regular Imperial troops working to evacuate citizens living in the floating island’s path. In an Elder Scrolls game, you’d get some of that, but not be able to hop from person to person chapter by chapter in the fashion the books do.

Umbriel slowly floats across Black Marsh, southern Morrowind and Cyrodiil with an army of zombies in tow, much like this article’s about to float into mildly spoilery territory for the two books. You see, The Infernal City and Lord of Souls outline what happened to cause the red year, a volcanic eruption which took the land of the Dark Elves from the beautifully alien place it was at the time of The Elder Scrolls 3 and reduced it to the ash-covered wasteland it’s outlined to be at the time of Skyrim. As the latter game’s lore books would subsequently set in stone, Baar Dau - the meteor suspended in the air above Vivec City at the time of Morrowind - fell and destroyed the city following the disappearance of the metropolis’ namesake ex-Tribunal god-king. The books reveal that the big rock didn’t fall the moment Vivec vanished, but was kept afloat by a device called the Ingenium, which is essentially a magic box powered by regular soul sacrifices. Two Dunmer, Vuhon and the aforementioned Sul, ended up having a fight rooted in the tech’s murderous nature and that’s actually what led Baar Dau to finally hit the ground.

Either way, the meteor falls, but that's not an insubstantial bit of backstory for a source outside of the games to add to the Elder Scrolls’ canon. Also wound into the tale of how Umbriel came to be is a bunch of extra flesh on the bone of the relationship between Daedric prince Clavicus Vile and Umbra. In the games, the latter’s always just been a powerful sword which imprints a new personality onto its wielder, but in the books it’s portrayed as a being capable of nicking some of Vile’s godly power and plotting to escape the prince’s realm of Oblivion via the building of Umbriel. Beyond those, the books also offer a chance to get to know emperor Titus Mede I, the warlord who took over the Empire following a post-Oblivion crisis interregnum and whose offspring you murder during Skyrim’s Dark Brotherhood questline.

None of this is anything close to required knowledge for playing Skyrim. No characters from the books pop up to say hello, likely because enough time’s passed for most to perish of natural causes. The sole reference I can recall comes via a chat about a location called Sleeping Tree Camp, which isn’t tied to any of the main questlines. You can, and I did for a long time, totally ignore these time-bridging tomes. That said, I do feel that having now taken the time to read them has helped me see the history of Tamriel as something not as strictly limited to the specific snapshots in time presented by each of the games.

Tales like these, which aren’t conveyed with as much natural emotional detachment as I tend to feel when reading much-condensed accounts of historical events or far off places on the pages of in-game lore books, really help in creating the illusion that The Elder Scrolls’ world is growing and evolving as our own does. It’s not just a snow globe that only shifts whenever some prophesied hero piloted by a controller or keyboard rocks up to shake it.

I do think, in large part due to the size of the real world gap between it and Skyrim, The Elder Scrolls 6 would have and still could benefit from having spin-offs like these to keep gently nudging the timeline forwards. A complicating factor is that judging by this week’s teaser, Sentinel seems like it could be set in the 206th year of the fourth era, a mere five years after the events of Skyrim. That’d mean no 200-ish years of wiggle room in which to slot some spin-off stories without serious risk of influencing things that’d have to be reflected in the new game. Unless Bethesda wanted to either put serious barriers up around where the spin-off could tread or get into a game of arbitrarily deciding what is or isn’t canon. With some collaboration, it could certainly be done, but it could also be a headache the studio wouldn’t want.

It’s likely too late to start the ball rolling now anyway, but that doesn’t stop it being worth asking why Bethesda and their famously adaptation-loving corporate bosses at Microsoft didn’t make sure they had something akin to these books in the works when Sentinel was punted down the road in favour of Starfield.

You did this well once, why haven’t you managed to pull it off again this time? I’m hoping that isn’t the inquiry which’ll come to define The Elder Scrolls 6 as much as questions about where a chunk of the old Bethesda magic had gone did with the studio’s trip to space. Lest the next long wait for a game from them be packed with even more uncomfortable silence.

#4049. "Arkane is profitable," say Marvel's Blade developers in fiery new statement, "just not profitable enough for Microsoft"

Unionised workers reiterate call for a "solid offer" for Arkane Lyon's future

Unionised workers at Dishonored developers Arkane Lyon have published a fresh statement about the progress of negotiations with Microsoft over the studio's potential closure. Aside from calling on Xbox management to make a redundancy offer proportionate to Microsoft's colossal market value, they accuse the parent company of creating the very economic conditions cited as a reason for closing Arkane, and thereby "sabotaging" development of the forthcoming Marvel's Blade.

Published by French union Le Syndicat des Travailleureuses du Jeu Vidéo - one of two unions who represent workers at Arkane, the other being Printemps écologique, who didn't issue a similar message - the official English translation of the statement begins by insisting that "work on Blade is going fine". It maintains that the game will measure up to previous Arkane Lyon releases, despite the stress of trying to pin down a new owner for the company, after Microsoft announced plans to part ways with Arkane and several other studios back in July. The writers then take Microsoft to task for making an "outrageously low" redundancy offer to Arkane's workers, and further accuse the Xbox company of essentially setting Arkane up to fail by imposing a hiring freeze and depriving the studio of resources.

"Microsoft chose to justify the closure on economic reasons," the workers write. "But Microsoft is actually why those economic reasons even exist." It asserts that Microsoft froze hiring "for 19 months, which artificially caused delay and additional cost", only to then use those delays and extra costs "as a reason to close down the studio". It also claims that Microsoft have "systematically" deprived Arkane of cash, by means of corporate mechanisms the statement doesn't make wholly clear. "Even this closure itself is done against any financial logic, as closing Arkane today would probably be more expensive than finishing the game," the statement adds, without going into detail.

"The truth is that Microsoft based its decision only on stone cold and inhuman logic, in which our lives, projects and dreams are voided, so we can better serve Microsoft’s short term financial goals," the workers continue. They accuse Microsoft of "the brutal application of a never-ending search for maximum profit optimization", citing years of mass layoffs across the Xbox company together with the recent voluntary buyout offering. "Arkane is profitable," they add. "Just not profitable enough for Microsoft."

The workers want a "solid offer" from Microsoft regarding the studio's post-Xbox future, declaring that "when the company who decided that Arkane has to shut down is, according to many sources the most profitable in the world, with a net profit of more than 133 Billions of dollars in the past years, it would be the bare minimum to ensure that the redundancy plan offered by Microsoft is on [par] with their means."

If Arkane have to close, the unionised workers call on Microsoft "to release funds commensurate with Microsoft’s status as a corporation, to make sure that the workers are compensated in line with the loss suffered". They'd like a redundancy payment of €200,000, two years of "redeployment support", a package of "shared resources for training and studio creation", including a residual bonus, and "compensation up to the redundancy payment for independent workers’ contract breach", to safeguard the livelihoods of freelancers and contractors.

The warring parties at Xbox and Arkane have until 11th December this year to figure out a deal. Reportedly, Ubisoft are among those looking to buy Arkane - a source of some concern, given that Ubisoft have also recently closed a number of studios and laid many people off. I'm not sure I'd be waving my wallet around if I were using my other hand to sign pink slips.
