#4048. "BioWare's closure represents an immense loss to and possibly a targeted attack on Canada's cultural legacy" argues petition calling on Canadian government to step in

1,662 Canadians have been verified as signing it thus far

Calls for the Canadian government to help ressurect recently shuttered RPG makers BioWare have progressed from a single post by a politician to a petition with enough signatures that it looks set to be presented to the Canadian House of Commons for an official response. So far, 1,662 people from the country of maple syrup and also other things have signed this call for their leaders to consider stepping in.

"BioWare is one of Canada's most important cultural exports to the world in the 21st century, selling tens of millions of units of their video games globally," declares the petition, started by Brendan Routh and authorised by Vancouver Kingsway MP Don Davies.

"BioWare's productions champion the values of inclusivity, tolerance, democracy, justice, and civil rights that are at the centre of Canada's national identity," its run of bullet points continues. "BioWare has been shuttered by its American parent company Electronic Arts, now owned by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund and Jared Kushner's Affinity Partners and BioWare's closure represents an immense loss to and possibly a targeted attack on Canada's cultural legacy."

With all of that in mind, the petition calls on the Canadian Government to "provide BioWare with the capital necessary to secure independence of themselves and their intellectual property from Electronic Arts and resume business as an independent, Canadian company". The Canadians who've signed also want their leaders to "protect Canadian businesses and cultural institutions from being dictated by American and foreign corporate interests" and "champion the values of inclusivity, tolerance, democracy, justice, and civil rights at the centre of Canada's national identity by preserving BioWare's invaluable contribution to the global entertainment industry".

Thus far, the petition's amassed 1,662 verified signatures from citizens across Canada, putting it above the 500 verified signature threshold required for it to be presented to the country's House of Commons. That'll be followed by the tabling of an official response from the Canadian government.

As with some of the responses from political bodies the likes of the Stop Killing Games campaign have gotten over the years, I find it hard not to see this petition not being greeted with an answer along the lines of 'We do care about this and thank you for raising it, but we're not really gonna do much here'. I think a full BioWare resurrection with government backing is highly unlikely, but finding some way to enshrine the studio's legacy or contribution to Canada's games industry and arts culture seems a lot more easily doable.

A big statue of Blokeshep and Femshep surrounded by their crew of potential allies somewhere in Edmonton, maybe. Or a big stone middle finger that's always required to be aimed at a poster for the next Star Wars film/game/TV show/bit of merch.

#4047. Poll: 15 Years Later, Is Skyrim Still One of the Best Open World RPGs Out There?

11/11/11 — the famous release date that will forever be associated with The Elder Scrolls 5: Skyrim.

If you haven't already realised, today marks the title's 15th anniversary, and it's crazy to think that the open world RPG remains one of the most consistently popular games out there.

Indeed, at the time of writing this article, Skyrim's racking up around 40,000 concurrent players on Steam. Again, it's 15 years old!

There's no denying that Skyrim has a unique magic to it; an atmosphere, a sense of time and place. Bethesda struck absolute gold with this one, despite its often obvious flaws as a role-playing excursion.

Of course, the fact that Skyrim's simply never been replaced probably bolsters its legacy. The wait for The Elder Scrolls 6 has felt eternal at points, and the long, long awaited sequel is reportedly still years away from release.

I mean, would you be at all surprised if we got a PS6 port of Skyrim before Sentinel's arrival?

But Skyrim also owes so much of its longevity to its players. Modders have kept the candle burning for over a decade, and people are still forging ahead with extremely ambitious projects today.

No game maintains that level of interest without being special in the first place, however. I'd argue that even now, there's no open world RPG quite like Skyrim — it's a truly timeless experience with regards to its gameplay loop, dynamic happenings, and player-driven sense of adventure.

I've seen Skyrim dubbed Distractions: The Game, and that comedic description still rings true. I've lost track of how many times I've started a new Skyrim playthrough over the years, but somehow, it's never lost its appeal — and that's primarily because of how freeform it can feel.

But do you think Skyrim still stands tall as an all-timer RPG? Dare I ask if you're still playing it in 2026? Vote in our polls, and then tell me all about your wintry adventures in the comments section below.

Robert (or Rob if you're lazy) is an assistant editor of Push Square, and has been a fan of PlayStation since the 90s, when Tekken 2 introduced him to the incredible world of video games. He still takes his fighting games seriously, but RPGs are his true passion. The Witcher, Persona, Dragon Quest, Mass Effect, Final Fantasy, Trails, Tales — he's played 'em all. A little too much, some might say.

Yes, Elden Ring, BotW/Totk, and Red Dead 2 have all improved on the immersive open world, but, again, Skyrim is a first person game and you’ve got far more agency in character creation.

Yes, you could argue that Baldur’s Gate 3 has more agency in creation, but, again, there’s something to be said about the first person perspective.

And, with Cyberpunk, you’re playing as V, not as your own very personal character. And honestly, I know there’s a lot of love out there for Cyberpunk, but I cannot divorce my experience of it from its launch status, which was more a comedy than a tragedy of sorts, but it’s not a game I have the love for that others have.

Do Oblivion and Morrowind have better main quests? Oh, absolutely. Fallout 3 and New Vegas may hold that honor as well. And, yet… there’s still something just a little bit more immersive about Skyrim. Fallout 4 didn’t quite replicate it and neither did Starfield.

What it is is the storysensing. Skyrim is the absolute master of this craft. Storytelling is a far more familiar concept, where you’re interpreting a story that you’re meant to experience, but storysensing is the concept of absorbing enough details in a game’s world that you personally tell yourself your character’s story. You subconsciously fill things in and create things mentally in the game that don’t exist, but mesh into the world. You become a character wholly of your own existence as you play and you experience quests as that imagined being would experience them. You choose good or evil. You choose to fulfill your destiny as Dragonborn or not. You choice the guilds you work with, to become a werewolf, a vampire, etc. And it holds up remarkably well today too. And even just a moment back in its world is strangely still as inviting and absorbing as it was all those years ago now. And let me also say that the game has an immense pull with all people, not just those of us that are dedicated gamers. Skyrim was the first game that my wife ever really loved and is likely the only game she will ever hit 100+ hours in. I’ll be honest and say it’s probably my only and last 1000+ hour game. My son is now able to sink into the game and appreciate its majesty and it’s not so complex a game, as many of the other games I’ve listed, that he is repelled from the game pretension. The game understands that it’s a game for everyone. It’s a classic, an all-timer, and it was obvious 15 years ago and it still is today.

Skyrim’s one of the greatest games of all time. Certainly in my personal top 10 list of games of all time. It does have its flaws, but they’re strangely something easy to overlook. I do find the main quest to have quite a weak third act, but yet I’ve been compelled to complete it more times than games with far “better” storylines. And perhaps time had been kind enough to give us some absolutely essential DLCs that do provide deeper storytelling that present epilogues just as immersive as base game. Skyrim is, basically, to video games what the Beatles were to rock music. You can argue why you think it’s overrated, but at the end of the day, it delivers so many hits and everything is so memorable, even though you can see its influences. Todd Howard was right back then when he said, “It just works.” It may have been buggy at times, but he was certainly right.

#4046. Shrek 2 Remastered Has No Official Reviews Yet, But The User Reviews Are Quite Bizarre

It has a high score on Xbox right now, but a Mixed one on Steam

Yesterday marked the launch of Shrek 2 Remastered on Xbox Series X and Xbox Series S (along with other platforms), and if you're wondering why nobody seems to be talking about it, it's because there are no official reviews yet.

It seems codes were only sent out at launch for this one, which means it's going to take a while for the critics to catch up and share their thoughts on this remaster of an original Xbox cult classic.

We can at least see what the initial user reviews are saying about it though, and if you look at the Xbox Store, everything seems to be pretty rosy. Shrek 2 Remastered has a 4.3/5 rating on the US Xbox Store as things stand, with 76% of people giving it a 5-star review, while most of the (minimal) grumbles are focused on bugs and crashes.

The Steam reviews for Shrek 2 Remastered are quite bizarre though. Over there, the game currently has a "Mixed" average rating based on over 350 user reviews, with 46% of people rating it "Positive" overall.

If you look at the "Most Helpful" reviews that appear first, there are multiple people suggesting it's not a great port, highlighting issues with bugged cutscenes, a lack of settings options, and even claims that the CPUs are less intelligent than they were in the original game (although others debate that it plays "exactly the same" as it used to!). There are also multiple accusations that the remaster might have been partially put together using generative AI, although this is just speculation and not confirmation by any means.

Some people are totally put off by all these issues, while others are still really enjoying their time with the game.

Satan Claus on Steam: "Shrek 2 was one of my favourite games growing up, and I honestly can't explain how happy I am to have the chance to play it again after all these years. It's just as special as I remember, and seeing it brought back with changes that do the original justice is wonderful. Even better, being able to enjoy it on modern hardware, especially the Steam Deck, feels like a dream come true. Some childhood memories are worth revisiting, and this is absolutely one of them."

Mikey on Steam: "I was really hyped for this remaster since this game is a game I grew up playing with my sister, but I am sort of disappointed with the state it is in right now. Lots of camera bugs, cutscenes ending aprubtly, missing skybox textures, characters looking woody and uncanny and lots more. It's like they just threw a paint bucket on it and called it a day. I'll wait for patches, since there still is hope."

As mentioned, Shrek 2 Remastered is getting a much better reception on Xbox than Steam right now, so perhaps we ended up getting the better version (or Xbox fans are more lenient), and you can check it out for yourself at the price of £22.49 / $26.99 for Series X and Series S if you're interested.

We do actually have a review copy of the game that we'll hopefully be able to check out soon, so stay tuned for our impressions in the near future. We'll also keep an eye out for raw Xbox Series X and Xbox Series S footage comparisons so you can get an idea of how it plays across both consoles.

For now though, we'll leave you with some basic gameplay from Shrek 2 Remastered down below.

#4045. You can now play Pillars of Eternity and Pillars of Eternity 2: Deadfire with a controller on PC from start to finish, thanks to a new update open for testing

Deadfire’s turn-based mode has also gotten a makeover

After gifting Pillars of Eternity a turn-based mode for its tenth anniversary, Obsidian have now rolled out full PC controller support for both the RPG and its younger sibling Pillars of Eternity 2: Deadfire. The support, along with some tweaks to Deadfire's turn-based mode, are currently out in public test form.

"You can now play the whole of either game with a controller, from character creation to the end credits (and, in Deadfire, all the way out to naval combat), in both real-time with pause and turn-based mode," the studio wrote in their announcement of the public test going live. "Deadfire’s support builds on the controller scheme from the console editions. Prefer to switch things up? Pick up your mouse and keyboard at any time, and the game follows right along."

"Deadfire’s turn-based mode has also been reworked with the improvements we made for Pillars of Eternity’s turn-based mode: turns now follow each character’s speed, combat is more lethal, and swapping weapons or drinking potions no longer costs your action. You can now switch turn-based mode on or off during a playthrough, and the update brings a long list of fixes across combat, quests, audio, and the interface."

Both Xbox and PlayStation controllers are included in the support, along with the Steam Deck and Steam's Big Picture mode. Radial menus have been worked in to allow rapid firing of abilities, spells, and party commands, with the interface also popping up the right button prompts for your controller of choice.

These additions are all part of Patch 1.3.10.0, the full notes for which can be found in the post I've embedded above, alongside instructions on how to get into the public test. The patch also does things like ensure "the description of Fulvano’s Boots is no longer fragmented". I'm glad Obsidian have saved those soles.

The studio haven't put a concrete end date on the test at this point, instead noting it "will run for some time as we continue to update it in preparation for a full release". As it's a test, those jumping in should expect bugs and other funkiness.

For players, the Xbox Series S is a great idea. A cheaper version of the console that sacrifices some power to reduce cost. On the development side, however, it's a different story, and longtime Tekken developer Katsuhiro Harada could do without it, and he has no problem saying so.

During a group discussion with other industry heavyweights at the SKY31 event in Seoul, South Korea, Harada quite literally used the opportunity to get his thoughts off his chest. "There's something I really want to say while I have the floor," he says, per InvenGlobal. "Since a senior Xbox official is actually in attendance here today, I wish hardware like the Xbox Series S wouldn't be released."

Tell us how you really feel, eh? He goes into his rationale after. "Low memory is an issue, but the hardest part is that it's a device so similar to Series X while having awkwardly lower performance," he explains.

"When porting to Switch 2, developers can shift their mindset to 'Switch 2 is a distinct device for Nintendo fans!'," he adds. "But with Xbox, after delivering your absolute best output, it feels like having to do extra work for a slightly weaker child."

I can see this perspective. The Series S requires its own particular round of optimisation, on top of whatever the devs needed to do to get their release working smoothly on the Series X. It's resource intensive, and another of the panelists, Pawel Sasko, associate game director at CD Projekt Red actually remarks that it "forces us to optimize our code very cleanly."

Harada's frustration is emboldened by the fact a lot of people use the Sereis S, especially stateside. "In markets like the US, there are more Series S users than Series X users, so we can't just cut corners," he says. "Yet after launch, Series S users direct their complaints at us developers rather than Microsoft, asking 'Why is texture resolution lower only on Series S?'"

Yeah, that would grind your gears. Sacrifices must be made due to hardware limitations, and studios can only do so much for their games. Getting something like Crimson Desert running on a Series S is no easy feat, and devs can only do so much.

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more

People should be aware of that before criticizing what they're playing. But more options are generally good, and a middle ground that's less cynical seems plausible here. Harada jokes about us getting a Helix S, and it just might happen. I look forward to his rant if it does.

#4043. Goddess of Victory: Nikke's PC launcher suffers potential malware infection, with its publishers suggesting folks who've booted since late September do a security check

A cruel twist for the Shift Up-developed epic shooter RPG of cruel humanity destiny

Goddess of Victory: Nikke, a gacha shooter/RPG developed by Stellar Blade makers Shift Up, has suffered a "security incident" which has seen its PC launcher potentially be infected with third-party malware. Thankfully, it seems a patch to make the launcher safe again has been quickly dished out, but publishers Level Infinite are still advising players who've booted the game up since September 27th to do some security checks.

"We have identified that some files in the NIKKE Windows PC launcher were recently tampered with by a third party, potentially allowing malicious programs to run when the launcher was launched," the developers of the game with anime girls who - judging by the promo art - breast boobily announced yesterday. "As a result, your PCs and account information may have been exposed to security risks.

"We are continuing to investigate the extent of the potential damage and review appropriate response measures. We are also conducting a thorough review of our network security environment, including our CDN, to determine how the PC launcher files were compromised. We will take all necessary precautions to prevent further damage and ensure that this issue does not happen again. We deeply regret that this security incident has caused Commanders significant concern and distress, when our responsibility should have been to provide a safe gaming environment."

In order to try and help players "scan for and remove the malicious programs distributed in this incident", publishers Level Infinite have added a feature to Nikke's official PC client that does just that. They're advising that anyone who's booted up the game at least once after September 27th at 15:41 (UTC+9) use that or perform a manual security check.

Once that's done, affected players are advised to change the passwords for any accounts they've used on the PC they used to boot the launcher, as well as generate new API keys and access tokens. "We take very seriously the possibility that this incident may have affected not only your gaming experience but also your PC, accounts with external services, and personal assets," Level Infinite added. "If you believe you may have been affected by this issue or suffered from any loss, please contact our customer support team. We will review each inquiry carefully and respond as promptly as possible."

Going forwards, they plan to improve their monitoring "so that any unauthorized file modifications or security threats can be detected early and addressed promptly", as well as "establish an integrity verification system for external resources accessed by the PC launcher" and ensure the launcher only requires "the minimum permissions necessary".

Here's hoping the studio are able to keep things more secure in the future and that affected players are able to get rid of any malware with minimal suffering or inconvenience.

#4042. 'We Will Put In Our Best Efforts To Develop For It' - Stellar Blade CTO Wants Xbox Helix Dev Kit

"Personally, I am looking forward to the next-gen Xbox"

Shift Up CTO DongKi Lee, best known for his work on Stellar Blade and the studio's mobile games, recently spoke at a developer panel about his excitement to get hands-on with Xbox Project Helix development kits. All whilst in front of a senior official of team Xbox.

As Inven Global puts it, Lee was one of five panellists, comprised of execs from other development studios, and answered questions on what it's like developing games for console in the Korean gaming industry.

When asked about what advantages the console platforms have compared to PC, fellow panellist and former Tekken CEO Katsuhiro Harada took the opportunity to throw some shade at the Xbox Series S, jesting "I wish hardware like the 'Xbox Series S' wouldn't be released", attributing additional development resources to optimising games for the lower spec console.

In response to this, the Shift Up CTO spoke about his excitement to work alongside Xbox and his eagerness to see Project Helix developer kits in Korea:

"Personally, I am looking forward to the next-gen Xbox 'Helix'. From an engineer's standpoint, if you provide us with a dev kit first in Korea as early as possible, we will put in our best efforts to develop for it."

Xbox players have been asking for a Stellar Blade port for quite some time, regularly mocking up fake Xbox Series box art and posting it to socials, and usually asking when Shift Up will bring the game to Microsoft hardware. It's certainly a possibility, and DongKi Lee's enthusiasm for working with Project Helix is encouraging. That, and this tweet from Edo, Shift Up's 'publishing guy':

During the panel, Lee was asked about the recent Switch 2 version of Stellar Blade and the effort involved in porting the game from PS5 to NS2. The Shift Up CTO shared a chuckle with the panel moderator and CEO Harada whilst discussing what could and couldn't be compromised during the port. Specifically, how reducing the polygon count on protagonist Eve's 'rear' was "never an option".

But I tend to agree with more with CDPR Associate Game Director Paweł Sasko that there are benefits for gamers with the Series S, and not just on the lower-end cheaper hardware itself, but by optimising for the Series S they can increase performance on Series X, PS5, PC etc.

@themightyant If they release a Helix S or something similar, it would be very different from the Series S from a developer's perspective. If I've understood things correctly, the Xbox Helix OS will be much closer to a Windows PC environment. That would mean developers wouldn't need to create a specific port for the Helix S, just like PC developers don't make a separate version of a game for every possible hardware configuration.

It would basically come down to a different settings profile that's optimized for the hardware. That's essentially how games work on devices like the Xbox ROG Ally. Developers don't make a special version for it, it's the exact same PC version, with only the configuration and performance settings changing.

I don't know exactly what the Helix OS will look like in the end, but there will almost certainly be a greater level of standardization between PC and Xbox games. The differences between the two platforms should end up being pretty minimal which would greatly reduce the amount of work developers have to do. Yes, it's interesting how Series S made developers optimise games and how those optimisations would later be used on weaker hardware like Switch 2 and Steam Deck. If Xbox games become just Windows games like any PC game, that would benefit Helix massively, and it could still run them with specific settings and optimisations added with that purpose.

#4041. Nvidia ensure unboxing a ludicrously expensive new graphics card isn't limited to real life in these RAM crisis times by releasing a GeForce 8800 GTX unpacking sim

Hey at least the card in this bit of 2006 nostalgia bait has only cost you a virtual arm and leg

In what feels a fairly cheeky move during a time when memory shortages have infamously made it pretty much impossible to buy a decently powerful new graphics card without spending approximately a gazillion pounds/dollars/dollarpounds, Nvidia have decided to put out a Steam demo that allows folks to re-live the feeling of unboxing a ludicrously expensive graphics card in 2006.

The demo, dubbed GeForce 8800 GTX - 20 Years of a Legend, has been developed by Dylan Browne. He previously made Through The Ages, a "real-time high end graphical cinematic that takes us on a nostalgic journey through three of NVIDIA's iconic GPUs" which is also on Steam for reasons.

The GeForce 8800 GTX demo, as you might've guessed, is a tribute to that specific card in the form of a tech demo simulating what it was like to unbox one in a mid-2000s bedroom. Seriously, there's a copy of Crysis on the desk so you know this is the domain of a true devotee to the best graphics available in around 2007.

"Step into a 2006-era PC gaming room, unbox the GeForce 8800 GTX, inspect it up close, and install it in an era-accurate PC tower," the demo's description declares. "Explore nods to GeForce history and hidden easter eggs as DLSS 4.5 with Dynamic Multi Frame Generation, Ray Reconstruction, path tracing, and Mega Geometry bring the nostalgic setting to life. From holding the card to the glow of the monitor, rediscover a moment in PC gaming history - or experience it for the first time!"

As the GeForce 8800 GTX was a top-line card that cost $599 on release in 2006 - about $1,000 in today's money if the online inflation calculator I've just used is on the money - this isn't really a 'we know cards are ludicrously expensive right now, but here's a reminder of when you used to be able to actually afford to unbox one' sort of demo. It is at least a free way to virtually experience having blown a chunk of your savings on something that can render really sexy textures without the existential dread of doing so in real life.

Well, I say that, I've just noticed the minimum requirements for the demo note that you'll need an RTX 4070 card. So, depending on your current setup, this might well be a case of Nvidia offering the chance to render unboxing a card you couldn't afford in 2006 via a card you can't afford in 2026.

Is that about the best we can all hope for in 2026? Probably.

Fields of Mistria's era of PC exclusivity may soon be over

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It sounds like Fields of Mistria, a gorgeous indie farming sim and RPG oozing with '90s anime vibes, is finally coming to consoles, as its devs confirm they've been exploring "other platforms" since its 1.0 launch earlier this year and that "porting work is actively happening."

Even as someone who plays games exclusively on consoles, I rarely find myself unable to play something I really want to, or, at the very least, not for long. However, Fields of Mistria has been an exception. Ever since its early access launch in August 2024, I've been yearning to dive into this gorgeous indie, and was admittedly rather heartbroken when its 1.0 launch came and went this summer with no mention of it branching out from Steam. Needless to say, I'm thrilled at the inclusion of three crucial sentences in a new blog post shared by developer NPC Studio.

"We're excited to share that we are exploring opportunities to bring Fields of Mistria to other platforms!" the devs begin. "We know many of you have been asking, and we've heard you loud and clear. While we're not in a position yet to confirm specific platforms and timing, we can confirm that porting work is actively happening behind the scenes."

Say it with me – finally. As NPC Studio states there, there's no indication of when this port might launch or which platforms it will run on, but rest assured, it's on the way. It's the sort of game I've always thought would be perfect for Switch and Switch 2 – like Stardew Valley and games like Animal Crossing: New Horizons and Pokopia Pokopia prove, there's something very cozy about being able to take a life sim around on the go with you (or curled up in bed), so that's what I have my fingers crossed for here.

Elsewhere in the blog, NPC Studio confirms that "we have plans for new content coming to Fields of Mistria in 2027, and we're excited about what's ahead!" The devs aren't giving any hints here, but will "be able to share more details" after they've dealt with other priorities, such as bug fixes, performance improvements, and finishing off localizations for the game's supported languages.

Be sure to check out our roundup of upcoming indie games for 2026 and beyond to see what else is around the corner.

#4039. Resident Evil Requiem Wins the First 2026 Game of the Year Award

Top accolade at the Golden Joystick Awards

Resident Evil Requiem has been crowned the Ultimate Game of the Year at the Golden Joystick Awards, the first major games award ceremony of 2026.

Alongside the biggest award, it was also named the Console Game of the Year, and it won categories celebrating the best lead performer (Angela Sant'Albano as Grace Ashcroft) and the best game trailer. Most of the Golden Joystick Awards are decided by a public vote, and the race for Ultimate Game of the Year was extremely close.

Resident Evil Requiem won the award with 17% of the overall vote, but Phantom Blade Zero was right behind it with 16% and then Crimson Desert got 15%.

Obviously, since it's not out yet, GTA 6 wasn't eligible for any categories.

Elsewhere, the award for the Best Remake / Remaster went to The Witcher 3 Remastered, then Dispatch won the Best Soundtrack and Best Storytelling categories. Onimusha: Way of the Sword has the Best Audio Design according to the voters, Valheim was the year's Best Indie Game, and The Witcher 4 is the Most Wanted Game.

#4038. Phantom Blade Zero is Steam's biggest launch of the year so far, selling over 4 million copies in three days

Phantom Blade Zero studio S-Game has announced that its debut title has sold more than 4m copies in its first 72 hours on sale. The game's official X account broke the news alongside a celebratory message, though without providing a per-platform breakdown of copies sold.

"Thank you everyone from the bottom of our hearts for all the love and support!" the developer wrote on X.

Phantom Blade Zero is available on Steam and PlayStation 5, but the 4m figure also includes sales made on the China-exclusive Tencent WeGame PC launcher. Prior to launch, Alinea Analytics analyst Rhys Elliott estimated Phantom Blade Zero to have sold over 1m copies before it had even released.

It was always clear the third-person character action game was going to be a hit, we just had to wait for actual figures to be released.

Phantom Blade Zero attracted over 431,000 concurrent players on Steam at launch, a figure that kept risking and rising into the weekend, ultimately settling at a massive 833,921 peak concurrent (via SteamDB). Just in case it wasn't already clear, this is Steam's biggest launch of the year so far, beating the likes of Forza Horizon 6 and far outpacing all other major releases such as Onimusha: Way of the Sword, The Blood of Dawnwalker, and Ace Combat 8.

Despite the very strong opening weekend's numbers, Phantom Blade Zero has not been able to match or exceed the performance of Black Myth: Wukong, 2024's also-Chinese developed triple-A action game, just yet. The breakout hit, estimated to have sold 30m copies since, is one of Steam's largest debuts ever, peaking at 2,415,714 concurrent players at launch.

In Eurogamer's Phantom Blade Zero review, Emma Kent spoke highly of much of the game, but was critical of its underwhelming narrative and lack of consistency, writing: "This game is exceptional in so many areas - the animations, the beautiful environments - and when the combat works, the sense of flow is incredible. Then you walk into a boss battle and feel all that power fade, like you're waiting your turn to get hits in with a wooden sword."

#4037. Apex Legends adds a grumpy, teamwiping Godzilla to its growing history of unappealing crossovers

No doubt eager as peas to help pay off EA's billions in debt, battle royale shooter Apex Legends is set to run another of its intellectual propertytastic crossover events. This one, starting on November 10th, stars Godzilla, of Godzilla Minus Zero, Godzilla vs. Kong, Godzilla (1954), Godzilla 2000: Millennium, Godzilla (1998), Son of Godzilla, and Godzilla (2014). I might be missing some.

Besides a profitable range of weapon and character skins, most of which appear to have hot glue gunned an 70-year film franchise's worth of dorsal fins all over themselves, the King of the Monsters himself will show up on the game's Storm Point map. He does at least have more than a background cameo: he'll occasionally blast an area with Legend-melting atomic breath, though brave souls who risk the danger zone can score a custom Devotion LMG with a unique heat ray attack of its own.

Worth noting also that the character skins are each based on a certain 'zilla movie, though as our freelance news writer and associate Large Lizard Cinema expert Ashley isn't working today, I'm not sure which of these are from hits and which are the duds. Walking wallhack motherfucker Bloodhound gets the newest fashion, their skin being inspired by Minus Zero, while my personal favourite Scottish scientist Horizon gets duds based on Big G in Godzilla vs. Destoroyah. Octane's skin is taken from... something called a Jet Jaguar? Google suggests this may in fact be elite Godzilla knowledge, something I clearly lack.

Regardless, and with the understanding that a lot of effort goes into these crossovers, I still kinda wish they didn't exist? Even putting aside basic game-playing problems with how, for example, wacky skins interfere with Legend silhouettes – you couldn't pay me to initiate a fight against a full team of near-identical Gundampeople - it's just icky to have an otherwise sharp, smart, at times fiercely competitive battle royale turned into an animated billboard for a few days.

Besides, Apex already has its own kaiju: the sleepy, pacifist Leviathans that innocently wandered into the King's Canyon map for a few of the earlier seasons. I consider these much better Friend Material than Godzilla, on the grounds that they'd only kill you by accident, and it was usually your own fault - by wandering under their briefly raised megahooves - anyway.

#4036. Soulframe to launch into free open alpha this week, as Warframe devs go head-to-head with WoW: Forever

Soulframe's Preludes (its own version of an alpha) is finally opening its doors to the whole world ahead of the Verse of the Veilands update. Starting this week, anyone who wants to can simply download the game and hop in, no invite required.

The date this happens is an interesting one: 6th November. That's two days after the release of World of Warcraft: Forever and the same week as Old School RuneScape's Hardcore worlds, so it's suddenly become a pretty packed month for MMO enthusiasts.

This comes after three years of closed testing for the fantasy action MMORPG, which players have been able to gradually see firsthand through sporadic invites. With Soulframe suffering delays since its first reveal, brief invite events have already occurred over this period. Even locked away, the game has received multiple substantial updates over the years, including new quests, Pacts (classes), factions and so on.

As for what newcomers to Soulframe can look forward to when Soulframe opens its doors, the Verse of the Veillands update is bringing a total overhaul of the map progression system this month. After the completion of an early quest, players are introduced to a corrupted landscape, the Veillands, which they must purify.

As you do so, new resources will be obtainable and side activities like fishing will be unlocked. You'll also be able to train up a small wolf pet into a full-on mount in the process. Previously, players were just thrust into the open world to explore and figure things out as they go, so this should provide something of an introduction to the game's open map. It won't be totally finished when released mind you, with updates to the Veillands system coming in the future.

On top of that, there's a new Pact called the Ode Shrike coming with the update. It's a tricksy trapper with spikes, balloon snares, bombs and chains to disrupt enemies as you whittle them down.

Could this be enough to win people over to Digital Extreme's newest project? Time will tell - but in the meantime its long-lasting sci-fi MMO Warframe is taking players to the Tau system in a major next step in the game's narrative this December. It comes with a detective noir inspired main quest, playable warframe, and even an in-universe Poker equivalent.

#4035. Two Major Developers Explain Why They Like And Dislike Making Games For Xbox Series S

"I wish hardware like the 'Xbox Series S' wouldn't be released (laughs)"

Over the years, we've heard all kinds of stories from all kinds of developers about whether they either like or dislike making games for the Xbox Series S, and former Tekken boss Katsuhiro Harada falls into the "dislike" category.

In a recent panel discussion that was transcribed by the folks at InvenGlobal, Harada noticed that a senior Xbox official was in the audience, and joked that he wanted to let them know how much he isn't a fan of the Xbox Series S.

"Since a senior Xbox official is actually in attendance here today, I wish hardware like the 'Xbox Series S' wouldn't be released (laughs)."

He then went on to explain that although the low memory is "an issue" of the Xbox Series S, the hardest part is that it's actually so similar to the Series X, but with "awkwardly lower performance". Harada also pointed out that players direct their complaints to the developers rather than Microsoft if they don't like the visuals and/or performance.

"Low memory is an issue, but the hardest part is that it's a device so similar to Series X while having awkwardly lower performance [...] Furthermore, in markets like the US, there are more Series S users than Series X users, so we can't just cut corners. Yet after launch, Series S users direct their complaints at us developers rather than Microsoft, asking "Why is texture resolution lower only on Series S?"

Finally, he also noted that developing for the Nintendo Switch 2 is actually easier in some ways because it's a "distinct device for Nintendo fans", whereas the Xbox Series S is akin to "having to do extra work for a slightly weaker child" compared to putting in your "absolute best output" for the Xbox Series X.

Despite what it might seem like, a lot of this conversation seemed to be very lighthearted and full of laughs, and when Cyberpunk 2077's Paweł Sasko stepped in to highlight the benefits of the Xbox Series S including its affordable price and the ability to better optimise for low-spec platforms, Harada admitted that he made it sound a lot more attractive.

In fact, it was so convincing that Harada jokingly worried that it might lead to a similar Project Helix alternative!

Director Paweł: "Harada speaks a lot of truth. Players don't fully understand the technical context behind why fewer characters appear on screen or why visuals are downgraded. However, intensely optimizing for lower-spec platforms definitely brings the benefit of making the game run significantly better across all platforms—including PS5, high-end PCs, and handhelds like Steam Deck and ROG Ally.

And the biggest advantage of Series S is that its affordable price makes it accessible. Not every gamer can buy expensive high-end hardware, so from a developer's perspective, even if the strict constraints are painful, there is a silver lining in expanding market penetration to deliver the game to more players."

CEO Harada: "Director Paweł packaged Series S so gracefully that the Microsoft representative in the audience keeps nodding along. I'm worried they'll feel reassured and release a successor like 'Helix S' for the next-gen Xbox as well (laughs)."

It's best not to take any of this too seriously, but it does at least highlight the differing opinions throughout the industry about whether the Xbox Series S was a good or bad idea in hindsight.

From a consumer perspective at least, we reckon it was a fantastic idea. The Xbox Series S has continually managed to deliver incredible-looking games over the past six years, and in a time where console prices are constantly on the up, the Series S at least provides a somewhat affordable current-gen hardware option - at least if you find a good deal.

#4034. The Legend of Khiimori's Mongolian Expanse update brings in frosty mountains and scorching deserts that'll require a lot more than a fur coat and a sturdy horse

Another day, another opportunity for some horsing around! I'm being literal here, to be clear, as a new update for The Legend of Khiimori dropped yesterday. It's called The Mongolian Expanse, opening up the map a whole lot more and making a sweep of other additions to the game.

Previously, you might have looked out unto the snowy mountainscapes and the scorching deserts and thought "boy howdy am I glad I can't go there, those temperatures look like a nightmare to deal with!" Well, good news, as you now can head to those locales, each with "their own waystations, Yam nodes, named places, chests and bandit caches."

You don't want to wander there without some amount of prep, however, as the mountains are cold and difficult to climb, with wolves none too kind to humans like you. The desert, of course, is really hot, for both you and your horse. Both additions remind me of Zelda: Breath of the Wild and its use of extreme temperatures acting as a sort of challenge gate. Neat stuff!

The buck doesn't stop there with this update though. You'll find a whole host of new wildlife, ranging from wild boars, to gobi bears and camels. Of course, a horse game wouldn't be one without more horse, which there is! It's a new breed called the Marwari, a horse that is "built for endurance and especially resistant to heat, a strong partner for long, punishing Desert crossings." Beyond that, you'll also find more than 60 new horse skills, all findable across specific regions and for specific breeds.

It's a nice beefy update with plenty more tweaks, additions and fixes on top of everything mentioned above. When it comes to the mountains and desert, you can also expect some big additions there, as this is only the first part of this update. You can read about everything else the update offers right here on Steam.

#4033. The Rings of Power's Dark Wizard reveal was one of the first things the showrunners wanted to do

Patrick McKay and J.D. Payne were eager to dive into the Dark Wizard answer

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Rings of Power showrunners say their fascination with revealing who the Dark Wizard is stemmed from some of their very first conversations about the show.

"The idea of Blue Wizards who went east is such a tantalizing piece of the lore," Patrick McKay told Radio Times. "It was one of the first things we talked about wanting to explore in the show – reaching that moment and figuring out who they were, what they were about, what happened to them, and his eventual fate."

After a brief interaction with the Secret Fire, Gandalf was gifted the knowledge of the identity of Ciaran Hinds' Dark Wizard. As some had speculated, he was the Blue Wizard Pallando, sent to Middle-earth to quell Sauron's rise to power – but his own murderous ambitions laid waste to Rhun.

First mentioned in appendices and notes to Return of the King by Tolkien, the Blue Wizards were expanded on slightly in the posthumous Unfinished Tales book. Since then, however, their role in Middle-earth's machinations have largely been untouched – and remain one of the franchise's great unanswered mysteries.

But Gandalf deepening his pool of knowledge from Middle-earth's First Age wasn't the only intention here. For those in charge, it was a perfect chance to dovetail Gandalf's own character growth with that as Pallando.

Fellow co-showrunner J.D. Payne said, "It also felt like an opportunity character-wise for Gandalf, because season one was about him figuring out who he is, and season two is how he controls his magic. In [season] three, the character has to go deeper because he realizes he's not just a human firework who can make sparks fly out of his staff, but that he has a prophetic register to his character."

Payne added, "It's a place where Gandalf's character journey meets Pallando's character journey and gives us a perfect opportunity to make a great story."

#4032. "We're doing great," says id Software boss, despite losing "about half of our studio" amid devastating Xbox cuts

Iconic Doom and Quake developer id Software was among the most heavily impacted Microsoft-owned studios during Xbox CEO Asha Sharma's devastating business "reset" earlier this year, with around 136 employees reportedly losing their jobs.

In the wake of those layoffs, id Software co-studio director Marty Stratton was recently asked about the current state of the developer, and how it has been affected by Sharma's cuts. "We're doing great," Stratton told journalists at a recent event (via IGN).

"Not to handwave the [layoffs] away… everybody knows we had about half of our studio exit as part of that," he continued. "But there was a very deliberate effort to make sure that we were incredibly viable coming out of that across everything we do, across game development and technology department."

This is not the first time a senior id Software member has pushed back on the narrative the studio has been "nerfed into the ground and gutted". Hugo Martin, id's other co-studio head previously claimed the remaining team is "the size we were when we made Doom 2016, and id Tech is very much alive and well".

Sharma's Xbox reset will ultimately see 3,200 jobs cut across Microsoft's gaming division, with many of those still to come. Those impacted by the first wave of cuts in July, however, included developers working on the id Software's id Tech engine. This is the engine behind all of the studio's games, and is known to be among the most performant engines, consistently producing visually-impressive games that require modest specs to run.

Following the layoffs, many inside and outside the studio said the id Tech team had been gutted. Longtime id Software programmer Chris Hays, who notably wasn't among those let go, said at the time, "It is hard to make a game that is triple-A, that is like we've done before, with half the people. And by hard I mean impossible". Hays also claimed "entire departments" and "entire disciplines" are gone.

While Stratton hasn't addressed those comments directly, he revealed id Software is now "working more closely than ever" with MachineGames, the Swedish studio behind the modern Wolfenstein games, and Indiana Jones and the Great Circle. "We've always had a very close partnership with [MachineGames], but I think we're at a point with technology development that both teams are incredibly talented and have incredibly talented engineers and we're really on an amazing path that had started pre-[layoffs]," he explained.

"We'd kicked this off earlier this year. We're really excited about that. We're both really really bullish on what we have ahead."

Id Software's next project remains unclear. MachineGames, on the other hand, recently said it's not done with Wolfenstein, so it's possible a sequel to 2017's The New Colossus is in the works.

#4031. After a 16-year long dev period, Faraway, a shooting star arcade game about siphoning the energy of other stars, is out now

Lord almighty, video games take a while to make, 'ey? Especially if you're just one person working on it by yourself. Such is the case with Faraway, out today, an arcade game that reminds me of the early days of PS3 indies "about a shooting star that creates constellations to stay alive," all made single-handedly by creator of cult-classic mobile game Eliss, Steph Thirion. Did I mention that Faraway took 16 years to make? Like I said, game development is a lengthy process.

Looking at Faraway, and knowing how long it took to produce, it doesn't surprise me to come from a dev who managed to release a mobile game in the early days of the platform, long before free-to-play got its chokehold on the industry. It also really does feel like it should be sitting amongst the likes of PixelJunk, this thing should be something I'm desperate to play on my PS3 while I wait for my controller to charge.

As mentioned, you are a shooting star, a "spark meant to shine and vanish in a blink." But still you persist, connecting to and wrapping yourself around starts to "harvest their energy," in turn lengthening your own life, and of course, in arcadey fashion, racking up a nice score. It looks like game design as poetry, everything you're looking at procedurally generated to bring freshness to every run. I can fully envision this as a "one more run" kind of arcade game, the best kind, especially in an age long past the need to shove in another of your hard earned coins.

Faraway conceptually charms me because it taps into a style of game we don't get to see much of any more. What I'm saying is, I'm just a teensy bit sick of how many roguelikes there are, but that doesn't mean I don't want a game I can just hop in and out of at my own whims. Sure, arcade games might not be in vogue, I just miss them a bit. In any case, Faraway is available to pick up on Steam right now. Seems like it'll be worth a punt!

#4030. 'You'll Own Nothing': Sony Wins Hall of Shame Award for Deciding to Kill Physical Discs

I can't imagine this is something Hermen Hulst will want to display on his mantelpiece: PlayStation and Sony have won a Hall of Shame award, called a Shonky Award, from an Australian outlet for its decision to stop making physical discs.

Choice, an Australian website, runs an annual Hall of Shame series, known as the Shonky Awards, where it highlights the "worst products and services uncovered by our experts this year". In 2026, PlayStation finds itself with a Shonky Award alongside Virgin Australia, Ticketmaster, and more companies.

This is because of the company's decision to end PlayStation disc production from January 2028, combined with its current EULA (End-User License Agreement) tied to digital game purchases. A lot of the Choice write-up focuses on the latter:

"In this age of instant gratification, it doesn’t get much more convenient than being able to easily download a movie or video game to your collection to start enjoying immediately," it opens with. "But will you be enjoying them for years to come? That’s less certain."

The site then continues: "Because, according to Sony Interactive Entertainment, you don’t actually own the movies and games that you buy as a digital download instead of a disc. Instead, you’re buying a licence to access the content via Sony’s various digital storefronts, such as the PlayStation Store."

News Sony Reminds PS5 Owners Their Digital Games Are Licensed, Not Sold

But Steam, Xbox, and Nintendo all say the same

News No Disc, No Buy and PS5 Blackout Protests Fail to Impact PlayStation

Active users increases, digital sales percentage increases

It speaks about how Sony still "owns your digital media", and how, in reality, you're actually buying a "long-term rental". Choice then points to the sudden removal of Studio Canal movies from the PS Store, where refunds weren't offered.

The decision to stop physical PlayStation discs is then discussed, with worries over digital ownership arising once more. It analyses the EULA once more, but as we've pointed out in the past, the terms of Sony's license agreement are virtually identical to that of Xbox, Nintendo, and PC platform Steam.

All their terms of use speak about how the content you're buying is a license — you don't own it. Allow me to reshare the research editor Sammy Barker put into his previous piece concerning the EULAs on other platforms:

The Content and Services are licensed, not sold. Your license confers no title or ownership in the Content and Services. To make use of the Content and Services, you must have a Steam Account and you may be required to be running the Steam client and maintaining a connection to the Internet.

All Digital Goods are licensed, not sold. Your right to access or use any Digital Good is subject to your compliance with: (a) all license terms, license limitations, codes of conduct, and payment terms in the Terms; (b) your payment in full for the applicable Digital Good; (c) these Rules, and; (d) any additional terms provided when you acquire your license.

Subject to the terms of this Agreement, Nintendo grants you a non-exclusive, revocable license to use the Software solely on the Console for your personal, non-commercial use. For clarity, the Software is licensed, not sold, to you, and you may not make use of the Software except as expressly authorized by this Agreement.

These all read very similarly and mean the exact same thing: on all the major video game platforms, you purchase a license to play a video game; you don't own the actual video game.

However, because Sony is removing the option of buying physical PlayStation discs in just over a year to channel all of its business into the PS Store, it's catching considerably more scrutiny than anyone else.

For that, PlayStation wins a Shonky Award from Choice.

"You can’t protect your licensed media based on the current EULA, and there won’t be any alternatives once the discs go away. You’ll own nothing," it concludes.

[source choice.com.au, via gamesradar.com]

Its always been this way - the terms haven't changed - the ONLY difference is that with Physical discs, that licence is embedded on that bit of plastic and you can sell, trade or let a friend borrow that Licence but with Digital, that licence is locked to your Digital account. Its a bit more tricky to block access to a Physical Licence but that hasn't stopped a number of games being 'unplayable' regardless of whether you bought a licence on disc or digitally - Destiny, Marvels Avengers, Anthem etc all now just coasters or 'landfill trash'.

What you purchase, as you always have, is a licence to access and use the Software belonging to a Publisher/developer on whatever platform you have. Just because you have a Licence to play BF6 on PS5, doesn't mean you can play on PC, Xbox or Steam as they'll sell you a licence to access that software on their Platform too.

Even back when games were supplied on Cartridges, you purchased a licence to play the Software loaded on to those cartridges. They obviously have to supply the software to you in some way so you can access it with your licence, but you don't 'own' the Software and if you tried to copy it and distribute it because you 'think' you own it, that's Piracy and always has been.

Not saying I agree with the way Digital is limiting customers ability to 'sell, trade or share' their Licence in the exact same way they can with Physical Not saying I am 'happy' that big Corporations are being more 'anti-consumer'. In theory, we 'should' own our Licences as we always have and should have the right to sell, trade etc but we've never owned the software and as games/hardware have become more integrated with the internet, its enabled the owners of that software/hardware to block or remove access. The Licence isn't as 'permanent' as it once was. You can still use your licence to play N64 games but many games or content aren't playable today even if you own the Disc because they've turned off the Servers - you can't play Killzone online anymore and like I said, can't play Destiny, Anthem or Marvels Avengers either whether you bought on disc or not.

#4029. In a world full of $200 controllers, this $35 Xbox pad manages to afford anti-drift sticks

The Drakong Challenger seeks to challenge expectations of what a pro controller should be priced at, as it hits the market swinging with features that you wouldn’t find on a first-party controller double its price.

Small and lighter than many other controllers

Why you can trust GamesRadar+ Our experts review games, movies and tech over countless hours, so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about our reviews policy.

Over the last few years, I have found myself gravitating further and further towards PC gaming, but after spending 8 hours at a desk all day at work, I don’t want to spend my downtime sat in front of a mouse and keyboard - I want to be firmly planted on my sofa with a controller in hand. The only downside to this is that the best Xbox Series X controllers that dominate the PC gamepad market can be expensive, so I needed something that offered as many features as possible without the price tag that comes with it. This is where newcomer brand Drakong comes in.

Drakong, a new peripheral brand owned by Hyperkin, seeks to give gamers like me the experience I crave but at a budget price; it strips away the fancy frills like RGB and wireless connectivity to keep the price down, while focusing on providing you with high-performing Hall effect sticks and triggers instead.

At a very reasonable price of $34.99 / £45, the Drakong Challenger certainly keeps its promise as a budget controller. But can the Challenger “challenge” some of its more expensive peers to be worthy of your hard-earned cash?

Like many of the best PC controllers, the Drakong Challenger has taken its design cues from Xbox’s iconic controller. The layout of the sticks is offset as you’d expect for an Xbox pad; it has the classic button layout and trigger position, and has the Xbox home logo front and centre to mark its official licensing from Microsoft. The only visual differences on the surface are the black shell, which features a print of green around the thumbsticks, and the M button, which I’ll elaborate on in a second.

On the back of the controller, the plastic is textured to offer some form of additional grip; jury is still out on how effective that is, in my opinion, but more on that later. Also on the rear of the pad are the back buttons. This is a must-have feature in my mind when it comes to being a pro controller in 2026 - I say that, but it should really be standard across all gaming controllers at this point, looking at you, Sony and Microsoft. Thankfully, mapping these is nice and easy without the use of companion software, because like any of GameSir’s controllers, the ‘M’ button I mentioned a paragraph back will help you tailor them to your needs.

One of the most noticeable aspects of the Drakong Challenger for me is how small it feels. While it visually looks the same as any Xbox controller, it appears to be slightly smaller, which can make or break how it feels in hand for gamers. In addition to this, it is also very light compared to others I’ve tested, like the PowerA Fusion Pro Wireless (645g), coming in at roughly 205g.

I can’t say the Challenger looks or feels “premium,” as it’s dressed in a fairly cheap-feeling plastic. This may be a turn-off to some, but maybe don’t expect too much more for the price.

Hardware nerds unite, sign up to our free tech newsletter for a weekly digest of the hottest new tech, the latest gadgets on the test bench, and much more from the team at GamesRadar+.

The standout inclusion for me is Hall Effect thumbsticks and triggers; especially in a budget option like this, it really speaks to Sony and Microsoft’s homegrown controllers costing more and yet sticking to their stick drift-prone potentiometer modules. Drakong opting for Hall effect in a more affordable alternative shows how easy it is, and will guarantee that you won’t get drift here.

Another key feature that I’ve previously mentioned are the back buttons; they feel nice and responsive and are placed in a really good spot for where my middle fingers rest on the rear of the controller. For something this cheap, it’s nice to see this feature being added.

I also appreciate the fact that the buttons are programmable without software; you simply press the ‘M’ button, and then press the button you want programmed. It vibrates to confirm it has worked, and then you’re good. While it isn’t documented anywhere when unboxing the controller, it’s pretty easy to work out.

Speaking of vibration, when I first picked up the Challenger and felt how light it is, I assumed it wouldn’t feature rumble. But to my surprise, when I programmed one of the back buttons, the whole pad shook in my hand. I feel like this is a feature that would be very easy for them to have cut to keep the price down and one that’s often missing in lighter gamepads, but I am glad it is here.

Given the price point, I was ready for there to be compromises when actually using the Challenger day-to-day, and I really put it through its paces across a number of titles - Assassin’s Creed Black Flag Resynced, Grand Theft Auto V, Resident Evil 2 Remake and The Blood of Dawnwalker. Across all titles, I found that the back buttons - like they are with most controllers - are the standout feature. They really elevate my experience when gaming, and it is no different here. They allowed me to really lock into the experience and gave me ways to tailor the way I play a game. My parries in Black Flag and Dawnwalker really benefited from this feature.

Thanks to the Hall Effect sticks and triggers, all of my inputs felt responsive and precise, especially when I was in the halls of the RCPD, and I needed to conserve ammo and pop heads. I had previously played through this game with my standard Xbox controller and found the experience here to be much more controlled. This extends to Grand Theft Auto V, where the triggers, while very responsive and sensitive, did allow me to very quickly accelerate and brake whenever a civilian decided to get in the path of my car - I’ll let you decide if I was speeding up or slowing down.

Having said that, I really don’t like the texture of the thumbsticks. They’re a soft plastic with a textured rim around the edge, but I found my thumbs slipping off them more often than not. I feel like they don’t provide much grip when using the pad and that’s something that is quite essential for playing games. When they worked and I could keep my thumbs in position, they were great, but I was really disappointed with how cheap this aspect felt.

This extended to the textured grip on the back; while I appreciate that it is trying to make it easy to hold the device, it didn’t stop the cheap plastic from sliding about in my hand. What doesn’t help this is the fact that it feels noticeably smaller in my hand than my go-to controllers - the PS5 DualSense Edge and the Power A Fusion Pro Wireless - so I constantly felt like I was holding a toy in comparison to what I normally use.

Across the rest of the Challenger, I found the face buttons and D-pad to be pretty standard; they provided me with good responses and nice tactile feedback. A nice surprise sitting at the bottom of the controller was the headphone jack; while I wouldn’t normally use headphones that are plugged into a controller, this is a nice addition if you want to plug in a mic.

I’d have liked to have wireless functionality included here, but I understand why it isn’t; they want to keep the cost down, and this is one way to do it. The USB-C cable provided is a good length and works, but for anyone whose PC is further away from their sofa and TV, it may be a little bit of a struggle to use outside of a desk environment.

I think the big selling point here is the fact that the Drakong Challenger isn’t going to break the bank; it’s $25 cheaper than the official Xbox controller, which is a whole portion of Avocado Toast in the current economic climate. For the price you are paying, you are getting a really good budget option that opens you up to some pro controller features.

For half the price, you’re getting Hall-effect sticks and triggers, and rear programmable buttons; unless you wanted something wireless, then for me it would be a no-brainer between those two choices. It’s really hard to beat the Challenger on a price-to-performance scale.

While it won’t be the controller I decide to use in my daily gaming life due to it feeling too small and light in my hands, plus finding the thumbsticks a bit uncomfortable to use, I can recognise that this would be a great purchase for anyone looking for a new controller… or has smaller hands.

I used the controller for a few weeks as my primary controller when playing games on my PC. I tested Assassin’s Creed Black Flag Resynced, Grand Theft Auto V, Resident Evil 2 Remake, and The Blood of Dawnwalker while using the controller.

#4028. Xbox Brings Its Free Tier Of Cloud Gaming To Loads More Players Today

You may recall that back in July, Xbox announced a new free version of Xbox Cloud Gaming that would allow you to play games at no charge, but you'd be forced to deal with ads as a compromise.

That tier of Xbox Cloud Gaming was in testing for months, but as of today (November 11th), it's rolled out publicly - meaning the vast majority of Xbox users around the world should now have access to it.

Xbox has been very quiet about it today so far, but based on what we've seen around the web, the free tier of Xbox Cloud Gaming will provide you with a 30-minute slot to stream "select games from your library" as well as select free-to-play games, after which time you'll be kicked off and will have to start a new session.

You'll see ads before the session begins, and seemingly never again throughout your 30-minute playtime.

"You can stream select games for free by watching ads before each gaming session. Session time limits apply. After a session ends, you can watch another set of ads to start a new session."

News Xbox Introduces Free Game Streaming With Ads, Outlines Five Principles They'll Adhere To

Rolling out now as a "test" for Xbox Insiders

Despite the rapid session length, this could prove a popular option for anyone who wants to play GTA 6 on Xbox One (for example) without being forced to pay anything for Xbox Cloud Gaming. We'd urge some caution for now though, as Xbox has yet to confirm whether GTA 6 will be one of the "select" games that supports this feature.

Meanwhile, the cloud playtime limits that were announced a while ago for Xbox Game Pass members have now started kicking in, which also means you can now purchase "Cloud Playtime" to top it up if you run out.

The prices for this here in the UK are as follows:

Curiously though, I've checked the new "Cloud Playtime" option in the Settings menu on my Xbox Series X and I'm being informed that I've still got "Unlimited" access to Xbox Cloud Gaming with my Ultimate membership, so it might be worth checking the same thing on your end and seeing what it says for you.

I'm not the only person who's spotted something similar:

Anyway, we've thrown Xbox's official tweet up above, and you can hit the link in it to find out even more details.

#4027. Over a decade later, Bloodborne remains so popular it reportedly sold a quarter of a million copies this year alone

Bloodborne, FromSoftware's singular Lovecraftian action-RPG, has reportedly sold more than 251,000 copies this year alone.

That's according to Alinea Analytics head of market analyst Rhys Elliott, who revealed the figure in a post on X, noting this brings Bloodborne's total sales up to an estimated 10.4m copies, generating $317m (around £236m) in revenue. Elliot also claimed more than half a million people played Bloodborne in October through PlayStation Plus.

Additionally, 12 percent of those are said to have played Elden Ring during the month, while 6 percent played Dark Souls 3, and 5 percent played Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice. There's a cohort of gamers who are always bouncing between different From[Software] games," Elliott pointed out. "Can't blame them, especially with this one."

Bloodborne is a PlayStation exclusive that sadly never left the PS4, despite consistent calls from fans for ports and remasters. While the game is playable on PS5 through backwards compatibility, Bloodborne barely benefits from the console's advanced hardware, only seeing smoother frame pacing. In other words, it's the same game with barely any perceptible upgrades.

Before Sony closed down Demon's Souls remake developer Bluepoint Games earlier this year, the studio reportedly pitched a Bloodborne remake, but original developer FromSoftware didn't want it to happen. When news of the pitch came to light, former Sony Interactive Entertainment Shuhei Yoshida said Bloodborne has a special place in director Hidetaka Miyazaki's heart and speculated the reason it hasn't had a remake is because Miyazaki would prefer to do it himself but doesn't have the time.

"Miyazaki-san really, really loved Bloodborne, what he created," Yoshida said at the time. "So I think he is interested but he's so successful and he's so busy, so he cannot do it himself, and he doesn't want anyone else to touch it."

Bringing Bloodborne back is tricky because "there's a lot of involved rights associated," according to former PlayStation boss

#4026. Ablahshikar is a maximalist, sickos only salvage-survival CRPG about ripping organs out of warships and pawning off strange goods that's now out in early access

I don't know what's going on, and I like it

Sometimes, you come across a game and instantly know it's for the sickos. Today that is Ablahshikar, a "turn-based salvage-survival CRPG adrift on the Candle Sea" where you rip out the organs of enemy warships to "rebuild your vessel into a doomed chimera," that is out now in early access. To be honest I could have just called it a CRPG and still labelled it as a game for sickos, yet everything that's going on here is obviously just doubling down on the sick factor.

Ablahshikar is a particular flavour of maximalism. Having not played it, it feels a bit impossible describe, I mean, just have a read of some of the game's Steam page: "Lo, destiny crooks a finger only to those whose eyes peer beyond þe next tempest. Take custody of a faltering war-barge that wanders the outer brine of Dastgerd. Thy wrists y-braced to a wan terminal of bone-whyte and tarnysshed latoun, þou steerest Ablahshikar by murke point-nettes and sputteryng tables." I don't know what any of that means! And I love it. Reminds me of Hylics in that the game's world is not translating itself for its audience; you take what you're given, and you figure it out yourself.

Judging from trailers and screenshots, there's a mix of activities to be getting on with. Occasionally you'll be piloting a strange, not alien, but definitely ancient ship of some kind in an arcadey sort of fashion. Then occasionally there's something that resembles Caves of Qud, i.e. some odd, 2D maybe dungeon crawling where your moves are dictated by individual keys on your keyboard. Then there's Disco Elysiumy cutscenes that feel like a video game designed in the year 1200 by someone from the year 2200, aesthetically anyway. As I said, it is a particular flavour of maximalism.

Truthfully, I do not know if I am sicko enough for Ablahshikar. Its mighty vision is terrifying, but I certainly am curious about it. Right now it's less than a fiver, and it'll only be in early access for roughly a couple of months where the price will then go up, so perhaps it's best to get in at the ground floor. If you are one such sicko, then you can pick it up on Steam right here.

#4025. As the controversy around AI-created video game copies continues, Anthropic seemingly restricts Claude's cloning abilities

An update to Anthropic's Claude AI software has seemingly blocked the creation of outright clones or copies of existing games. Instead, Claude has been altered to only create "original" games.

Among the first to share news of the change was X user Chasm, who posted a screenshot showing the new rule, purportedly added around 27th October. "Do build original games, games in a genre, and games from the user's own designs and assets," it reads. "Don’t build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is renamed or called original.”.

While Anthropic is yet to issue an official statement on the new rule, technical staff member Addy Osmani commented beneath Chasm's post, confirming the change's legitimacy. He noted it was included because "using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy", but added that creating original games and those built with a user's own assets should still be possible.

Following the new rule's inclusion, users on GitHub shared newfound barriers they'd run into as a result. Reports included being blocked from creating digital modules for board games, and from recreating a commercially produced board game for personal use. Eurogamer has contacted Anthropic for comment on the rule change and its stance on AI game copies.

The modifications to Claude have appeared at a time when AI copies of games have drawn increasing ire, with game communities pushing back against them and developers pulling public-facing demos in fear of having their work stolen. AI-assisted copies of triple-A games have also emerged, including a version of Mario Kart 8 playable in an internet browser. However, this was taken down in a matter of days, presumably thanks to a legal notice from Nintendo.

Of course, even if Claude is prevented from making game copies, other AI tools, such as Deepseek, still lack similar restrictions. Until such measures are ubiquitous, the issue will continue. Given Claude's position as one of the most popular commercial AI tools out there, however, this will certainly make a dent in the problem.

#4024. BioWare are gone, but at least you'll be able to watch their final days in a documentary next year and oh wait that's really sad actually

It feels like every single week for the past few years has been the infinitely quotable 30 Rock quote on repeat. That feeling struck particularly last month when EA decided to shut down the iconic Mass Effect and Dragon Age developer BioWare. That obviously resulted in the cancellation of Mass Effect 5, of which a leaked trailer and some, now former, devs made sound pretty interesting. But hey! At least there's a documentary coming next year all about the studio that managed to capture the studio's last days! Yeah, I'm not so convinced by this upside either.

As reported by Deadline, Shane Fennessey and Adam Scorgie will be helming a documentary about the beloved RPG studio for Canada's Super Channel. It's called, punnily enough, Massive Effect: The BioWare Story, and will apparently take a look at its origins in 1995 all the way up to its closure and a bit beyond, planned for release in 2027. Filming began two years ago, so clearly this was meant to be much more of a celebratory project than the funeral procession it's going to be.

Some big names from BioWare's history will be appearing in the doc, including its founders Ray Muzyka, Greg Zeschuk and Augustine Yip, alongside the likes of longtime devs like Mark Darrah, David Gaider, Drew Karpyshyn, Aaryn Flynn, Mac Walters, Trent Oster, James Ohlen and Caroline Livingstone. You can also expect appearances from Jennifer Hale, Casey Hudson and, as if his sole goal is to haunt this industry everywhere, Geoff Keighley.

In a statement, co-founders Muzyka and Zeschuk said, "When the production team asked for our blessing to tell the BioWare story, we were honored and deeply moved. BioWare was never just about the logo or the building. It was about the stories brought to life by the amazing people on our dev teams, and the fans who defended those worlds, championed them and carried them forward. We’re proud this film honors those who made it all possible. The best stories never really end. They live on in our memories and wait for someone to pick them up again."

Obviously the documentary won't only be about the studio's closure, it sounds like a much bigger effort than that, so hopefully it will be a way to recognise how much of an influence BioWare has had on RPGs. It's just a ridiculous shame that it's something of a posthumous release. Continued solidarity with all those at BioWare.

#4022. 'There Is No Truth to These Claims': Marvel 1943 Not Cancelled, But Doesn't Sound Great

Marvel 1943: Rise of Hydra – the highly promising superhero game starring Captain America and Black Panther – has not been cancelled, despite rumours to the contrary earlier today.

A fan account claimed on X (or Twitter) that the project, fronted by former Uncharted lead Amy Hennig, had been scrapped. That post has since been deleted.

But Kotaku gained access to a message posted in dev Skydance Games’ private Slack channel, where executive producer Lu Gigliotti confirmed with leadership that the reports aren’t true.

The game – first announced in 2019 – was originally due out earlier this year, but has now been pushed back to 2027.

And based on further reporting from Kotaku, you may not want to get your hopes up too high for this one.

While the project is purportedly progressing and is poised to hit an “alpha” milestone soon, it’s allegedly over budget and has been scaled back significantly.

Curiously, journalist Rebekah Valentine reports that the title was originally intended for Netflix, but transitioned to consoles like PS5 during development.

As such, gameplay is said to be light, “primarily using only one button and lacking significant interaction”.

If you felt this year’s Marvel’s Wolverine was a bit basic, then it sounds like this may end up even more simplistic by comparison.
